studies.title: A Call Made Quietly
studies.meaning: The surah opens with five disconnected letters, and the classical commentators record that their meaning is not known with certainty, most preferring to say God knows best rather than to choose among the proposals. What follows names the subject of the whole chapter: a mention of your Lord's mercy toward His servant Zechariah. Then a single detail is given about how he prayed. The call was hidden, made where nobody could hear it, and that quietness is the first thing the surah tells you about him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the middle years, and the classical sources connect this surah with the emigration to Abyssinia, reporting that passages from it were recited before the Christian ruler there. Whether or not that account fixes its date, the surah's content fits a moment when the small Muslim community needed the stories of earlier prophets and the common ground with people of the earlier scriptures.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both remembering and speaking aloud. Placing it at the head makes the whole chapter an act of recalling, which is why the surah keeps repeating the instruction to mention this or that figure in the Book.
The noun for calling out to someone at a distance, usually loudly. Pairing it with the word for hidden makes a deliberate tension: the reach of a shout with the volume of a whisper.
Concealed from others rather than merely quiet. The commentators read it as prayer made where no one could observe it, which they treat as the reason it is singled out for mention here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Privacy was scarce in the seventh century. Houses were shared, courtyards were open, and worship in Mecca happened in view of the sanctuary and everyone circling it. To pray unobserved took effort: a corner of a house at night, a walk out past the last dwellings. The early Muslims in Mecca knew this exactly, since for a period they prayed in ravines outside the city to avoid being seen.
studies.didYouKnow: Twenty-nine surahs open with disconnected letters, and only two of them use five. This is one, and the other appears near the start of a surah later in the Book. The classical tradition preserved the letters exactly as recited without settling what they mean, which is itself notable in a tradition that comments on almost everything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Opening a chapter of mercy with letters nobody claims to understand sets a tone the surah keeps. Something is given, it is genuine, and it is not fully available. The detail about the hidden call then makes a claim about prayer itself: the value of the asking is not in its being heard by anyone present. A call made where no one could hear it is chosen as the example, and what follows shows it answered.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same prayer of Zechariah and the same sign, in a different surah's telling.
Records the same request in two lines and notes that he called on his Lord in longing and awe.
Instructs the reader to call on the Lord humbly and in secret, the manner described here.

studies.applyIt: Make one request this week that nobody else knows about. Not a private version of a public plan, something you have told no one and will not mention afterwards. The surah opens by singling out a call made where nothing could be heard, and there is a particular honesty available in a prayer that has no audience at all.

studies.title: My Bones Have Grown Weak
studies.meaning: A prayer that begins with an inventory of failure. Zechariah names his bones as gone soft and his head as set alight with white hair, an image of grey spreading like fire. Then he gives his reason for asking, and it is not his merit but his record with God: he has never been disappointed in calling on Him. The commentators note the sequence, weakness first and confidence second, as the shape of the request.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah revealed in the difficult middle years, and the one recited before the Christian king of Abyssinia by believers who had fled there. The surah opens with this prayer of Zechariah and moves through Mary, Abraham and Moses. No occasion is reported for the ayah itself. Placing an old man's plea at the head of the surah sets its register, which is intimate rather than argumentative.

keyTerms.note: A verb for losing structural strength, used of a rope or a wall. Applied to bone, the hardest thing in the body, it names the failure of the last thing a person expects to give way.
The verb for kindling. Grey hair is described as a fire taking hold of the head, which carries both the whiteness and the way it spreads without being stopped.
A word for someone who ends badly or comes away empty. Saying he has never been that in calling on God turns a lifetime of answered prayers into the ground for one more.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Old age without an heir was a specific kind of ruin. Property, water rights and a family's standing passed through sons, and a man who died without one watched his line close in his own lifetime. Care in old age also came from children and from nobody else. The audience hearing Zechariah's prayer knew exactly what he was asking for, because they had all seen a household end that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah before this one describes his call as made in secret, and the word used suggests something close to a whisper. He is alone, he is old, and he is quiet. Commentators have long paired that detail with the fact that the answer, when it comes two ayat later, is addressed to him by name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer models something unusual: it argues from past answers rather than from present deserving. That treats the relationship with God as having a history a person can appeal to, which is a warmer idea than either bargaining or bare submission. It also shows a prophet stating his physical decline plainly to God, without piety about accepting it. Nothing in the ayah suggests that naming what has failed is a lapse in trust.

crossReferences.why: The same prayer told again, with the sign of three days of silence.
A shorter version, closing on how the three of them called on God.
Jacob, also old and bereaved, refuses to despair of God's relief.

studies.applyIt: Try praying for something today by first telling God, honestly, what is not working: the knee, the money, the child who will not speak to you. Then say what Zechariah said, that you have called before and it has not gone badly. The order matters. He named the weakness first and the confidence second, and the request came after both.

studies.title: A Name Never Given
studies.meaning: The request is stated with its reasons intact and none of them softened. He fears what his relatives will do after him, his wife has never borne a child, and so he asks for someone from God's own side. What he asks for that heir is not wealth or standing but that he inherit prophethood and be pleasing. The answer comes without preamble, addressing him by name, and adds a detail nobody requested: the boy has a name, and no one before has been given it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Zechariah served at the sanctuary in Jerusalem in the generation before Jesus, and the Quran assumes an audience with some knowledge of him. The commentators read the fear about his relatives as concern for what they would do with the religious trust he held rather than with property, since the inheritance he asks for is described in terms of the house of Jacob.

keyTerms.note: A form used of both women and men, from a root about cutting off and leaving fruitless. It is stated flatly here, as one of the reasons given, rather than being avoided or worked around.
The word covers both succession and closeness, since in Arabic the one who inherits is the one nearest. He is asking for a successor and for kin in the same breath.
One who shares a name with another. It occurs twice in the Quran and both are in this surah, once of a name never given to anyone before and once in a question about God having any namesake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names in Arabia ran in families, and a child was usually given a grandfather's name or the name of someone in the clan worth remembering. To be told your son's name is one nobody has carried would have registered as strange before it registered as an honour. Inheritance was equally concrete: who took over a role, a herd, a debt or a trust was settled by kinship, and a childless man watched that pass to cousins.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a namesake occurs exactly twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. Here it says nobody had been given this child's name before him. Later in the same chapter it appears in a question about God, asking whether you know of any namesake for Him. The same rare word marks a unique human name and an incomparable divine one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer models something the tradition has drawn on since: reasons are given honestly, including the ones that make the request look unreasonable. Nothing is hidden to make the asking easier. What is asked for is also specific about the right thing, since the concern is for what he holds rather than for what he owns. The answer then exceeds the request in a small way, by naming the child, which is the surah's first instance of a pattern it repeats.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same request and the same answer, with the angels calling out while he stood praying.
Records the prayer and adds that his wife was made fit for him, and that they hurried in good works.
Uses this passage's rare word for a namesake again, there asking whether God has any.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something this week and give the honest reasons alongside it, including the ones that make it sound unlikely. Say the whole thing to God as it actually stands, without editing it into a more reasonable request. Zechariah names his age, his wife's barrenness and his fear of his own relatives, and the answer arrives anyway.

studies.title: When You Were Nothing
studies.meaning: The answer has come and the question that follows is not doubt but astonishment, and the commentators are careful to distinguish them. He restates the two obstacles, his wife's barrenness and his own body worn down past use. The reply reports God's own words and does not address the obstacles at all. It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were not a thing. The argument is from his own existence, which he had never thought of as needing explaining.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note that this exchange runs almost word for word alongside the one that comes later in the surah with Mary, and read the pairing as deliberate. Both are told the same thing, that it is easy, and both are answered from the same direction. The surah is establishing a pattern before it reaches its most contested moment.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative asking about the manner or the way of a thing rather than about whether it is so. Arabic grammarians note that it does not carry denial, which is why the commentators read the question as wonder rather than doubt.
From a root about going past a limit, used of bones grown brittle and wood gone dry. It occurs twice in the Quran, both in this surah, and the other use is of stubborn defiance.
Not merely possible but light, of little weight. The word measures the act against the actor rather than against the obstacle, which is why the reply does not engage with the difficulties he listed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was visible and final in the seventh century. There was no way to slow it and no way to conceal it, and a man past a certain point was carried by his sons or he was not carried at all. Childlessness in that world was not a private disappointment but the end of a line, a name and a household. The reasons Zechariah gives are the two most obviously conclusive facts of his life.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this passage uses for old age that has passed every limit occurs twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. Here it describes a body worn out. Later it describes people most stubborn in defiance of the Most Merciful, using the same root. The vocabulary of a limit overshot covers both a man's bones and a person's insolence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes a way of arguing that the Quran uses repeatedly: the questioner is sent back to his own existence. Since he was once not a thing at all, the distance from nothing to him is greater than the distance from him to a son. That converts an appeal to power into an appeal to memory. It also treats the question kindly, since nothing in the answer suggests the astonishment was a fault.

crossReferences.why: Mary asks the same kind of question later in this surah and receives the same phrase in reply.
Opens with the same idea, a stretch of time when the human being was not a thing mentioned.
Tells the same exchange with the reply that God does whatever He wills, and gives the sign.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the least likely thing in your life that is now ordinary: being born at all, meeting the person you live with, the work you do. Pick one and trace how thin the chain was. The reply here does not argue about the future. It sends a man back to look at what has already happened to him.

studies.title: Three Nights Without Speech
studies.meaning: He asks for a sign and receives one that costs him something. For three nights he will not speak to people, while remaining otherwise sound. Commentators note the last word carefully: nothing is wrong with him, the tongue simply will not move for ordinary speech. Most read the restriction as covering talk with people while leaving remembrance of God open, so what is taken away is exactly the part of speech that is spent on others. The sign is not a display. It is a silence only he would feel.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Zechariah held a religious office in Jerusalem that involved leading and instructing people, so a sign of this kind fell directly on his working life. The commentators note that a parallel account in another surah gives the period as three days rather than nights, and treat the two as describing the same span from different ends rather than as a discrepancy.

keyTerms.note: The same word the Quran uses for its own verses and for the wonders of creation. Asking for one is asking for something that points beyond itself, which is why the answer given is not a demonstration of power.

A form implying exchange with another party rather than mere utterance. The restriction is therefore on conversation specifically, which is how the commentators read the exemption of remembrance from it.
Whole and properly formed, with nothing missing. It occurs four times in the Quran and three of those are in this surah, where it marks bodies and forms that are exactly as they should be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man in Zechariah's position lived by speaking. Teaching, judging disputes, leading prayer and answering questions were all done aloud and in person, since almost nothing was written and no one could have read it if it were. Losing conversation for three days meant a household run by gesture, a role suspended, and every explanation deferred. It was a sign that could not be shown to anyone but was impossible to hide.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for being sound and whole occurs four times in the Quran, and three of them are in this surah. It appears here of a man whose speech stops while his body stays intact, later of the messenger who comes to Mary in the form of a well-made human being, and later still of a level path, in Abraham's appeal to his father.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sign given is the opposite of a public wonder. It works inward, and it takes away the faculty by which a man in his position exercised his role, so that for three days he could do nothing but receive. That fits the surah's opening, where the prayer singled out for mention was the one nobody heard. Confirmation, in this account, arrives in the same register as the request: privately, and at some cost.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sign as three days, with the instruction to signal rather than speak.
Has Mary told to keep a fast of silence later in this surah, in a very different situation.
Shows the sign taking effect immediately, as he comes out and can only gesture to his people.

studies.applyIt: Take a few hours this week without speaking to anyone: no calls, no messages, no comments under things. Keep working, keep walking about, just do not put anything into words for other people. Most of us discover we were talking to fill something. Notice what turns up in the space, and whether you wanted it there.

studies.title: Tenderness From Us
studies.meaning: The sign takes effect at once: he comes out and can only gesture to his people to praise God morning and evening. Then the child is addressed directly, told to take hold of the Scripture with strength, and given judgement while still a boy. What follows is a list of what he was given, and the first item is unexpected. Tenderness, from God's own side, listed among gifts alongside purity. Commentators note that the qualities named are not achievements but things placed in him, and that the last line rules out two faults by naming them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. John lived and preached in the region around the Jordan in the years before Jesus began his mission, and the Quran assumes an audience with some awareness of him. The commentators do not give an occasion for these ayat and read them as part of the surah's opening sequence, which sets out one answered prayer in full before turning to Mary.

keyTerms.note: The phrase for taking hold of something with determination rather than lightly. It is used elsewhere of receiving scripture, and it treats holding a book as a matter of grip rather than of understanding alone.
From a root about yearning, used of a she-camel calling for her calf. It occurs only here in the entire Quran, and it names a warmth of feeling as something granted rather than developed.
One who compels others, from a root about forcing something into shape. The Quran uses it for those who dominate people, and its denial here is paired with the denial of disobedience to parents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian culture praised a certain hardness in men: endurance, pride, readiness to answer an insult. Tenderness was a word for mothers and for camels with young, and a list of a man's virtues would not usually have included it. Placing it second in a prophet's description, before devoutness and before kindness to parents, would have registered as a reordering of what a strong man is.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for tenderness in this passage occurs only once in the entire Quran. Arabic lexicographers connect it with the sound a she-camel makes calling for her calf, so the root is drawn from animal affection rather than from human sentiment. Of all the qualities the Quran attributes to a prophet, this one is named a single time and never used again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lists character as gift rather than as attainment, which changes how the reader is meant to hold it. Wisdom, tenderness and purity are described as given from God's side, and what remains for the person is to receive and to hold firmly. The final line then defines goodness partly by absence: not overbearing, not disobedient to parents. A prophet is described by what he was not made into as well as by what he was.

crossReferences.why: Describes John with a different set of qualities, confirming the word of God and a chaste prophet.
Uses the same phrase for taking hold of what was given with strength, addressed to a whole people.
Has Jesus described in the same terms later in this surah, dutiful and not overbearing.

studies.applyIt: Look at the list in this passage and notice that tenderness sits near the top. Then think about the qualities you would name if someone asked what you were working on in yourself. If softness toward people is not on that list, add it this week, and pick one person to practise it on who does not make it easy.

studies.title: She Withdrew To The East
studies.meaning: Peace is pronounced over John at three points, birth, death and being raised, and the account closes. Then the surah turns with an instruction: mention Mary in the Book. What is given first is a movement away. She withdrew from her family to a place to the east and put a screen between herself and them, and only then was the spirit sent to her, appearing as a well-formed human being. Commentators note the sequence. The withdrawal comes first, and the visitation happens inside it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report that this surah was recited before the Christian ruler of Abyssinia when Muslims sought refuge there, and that its account of Mary and her son formed the common ground on which they were received. Whether or not that fixes the date, the surah devotes more space to Mary than any other passage of the Quran and names her more often than any other woman.

keyTerms.note: From a root about casting something aside, so a deliberate separating rather than a drifting away. The same verb returns later in the surah when she withdraws again, carrying the child, to a distant place.

Anything placed between two parties to block sight. Here it marks a chosen privacy rather than a requirement, and the Quran uses the same word for barriers between people and things they cannot perceive.

The commentators overwhelmingly identify this with the angel who brings revelation, though a minority read it differently. The possessive keeps the sending entirely on God's side, which the following ayat make explicit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Solitude for a young woman was almost unavailable in that world. Households were extended, work was communal, and water was drawn where everybody gathered. To go apart deliberately, to the east of a settlement and behind a screen, meant leaving the only structure that gave a woman standing and safety. It was an unusual thing to do and would have been noticed, which is part of what the later ayat turn on.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran. Other women appear as the wife, the mother or the sister of someone, but her personal name is used, and it appears in more than thirty ayat across the text. One surah carries her name, and this one gives her story at greater length than any other passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The peace pronounced over John at three points is echoed almost exactly later in this surah, where Jesus says it of himself, and the parallel draws the two accounts into one shape. What follows about Mary makes a claim about how encounter with God happens. She is not interrupted in the middle of her life; she has already stepped out of it. The passage does not present that as a condition, but it does place it first.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same threefold peace, there spoken by Jesus about himself, later in this surah.
Gives the angels' address to Mary, telling her she has been chosen and purified.
Describes her guarding her chastity and confirming the words and books of her Lord.

studies.applyIt: Put a screen of your own up for an hour this week: no phone, one room, door shut, nothing to answer. Do not plan what to do in it. The passage puts the withdrawal before anything else happens, and most of us have arranged our days so that the withdrawal never comes at all.

studies.title: I Take Refuge In The Merciful
studies.meaning: A stranger has appeared where nobody should be, and her first words are not a question but a taking of refuge. She names the one she is sheltering in and then adds a condition aimed at him: if you are someone who guards against God. Commentators note that she appeals to his own conscience rather than calling for help, which is the response of someone with no other protection available. He answers by stating what he is and what he brings, and her second reply gives the two facts that make the announcement impossible.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators place Mary in the care of the sanctuary at Jerusalem, set apart for service there, and read her withdrawal as ordinary within that life rather than as flight. Nothing in the classical accounts suggests she expected a visitor. The surah gives her words in full, including the fear, and the sources treat that as part of the point rather than as detail to be smoothed away.

keyTerms.note: The verb for running to something that can shelter you, used of a person reaching a stronghold. It is the same word that opens the formula Muslims say before reciting, and it names an act rather than a feeling.
She chooses this name rather than any other. The surah uses it repeatedly, more than most chapters do, and choosing mercy as the name to shelter under is itself part of what she says here.
From a root about exceeding a limit or seeking beyond what is allowed. Her denial covers not only the act but the character, so she is answering a charge nobody has yet made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman alone with an unknown man had one thing to lose and no way to get it back. Reputation was the whole of a woman's security in that world; a doubt could not be argued down once it had started moving through a settlement, and her family bore it with her. Her first sentence is not fear of harm in the moment. It is the reflex of someone who understands precisely what is now at stake.
studies.didYouKnow: The name of God that Mary chooses for her refuge appears in more ayat of this surah than of any other chapter in the Quran, thirteen in all, more than double the next highest. The Quran elsewhere records that the name was unfamiliar enough to some in Mecca that they asked what it meant, which makes its concentration here all the more marked.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Her appeal establishes something about refuge itself. She is physically alone, with no one to call and no way to escape, and the protection she reaches for is not rescue but a name spoken into the situation. The passage also records fear in a figure the Quran holds in the highest honour, without treating the fear as a lapse. Being chosen does not exempt anyone from the ordinary human response to danger.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same announcement and the same question in another surah's telling of it.
Uses the same verb for taking refuge, there as what precedes the reciting of the Quran.
Uses the same root for taking refuge in Joseph's answer, at a moment of exposure of his own.

studies.applyIt: Learn one short phrase of taking refuge and use it the next time something startles you, before you decide what to do. Not as a charm and not instead of acting. The point is the order: Mary speaks the name first and then deals with the situation, and having a first sentence ready changes what the second one is.

studies.title: A Matter Already Decided
studies.meaning: The answer to her objection is the same one Zechariah received a few ayat earlier, word for word in its central phrase: it is easy for Me. Then two purposes are given, and both point outward. The child will be a sign for people and a mercy from God, so he is not described as a reward to his mother but as something the world will need. The last clause closes the exchange rather than continuing it. The matter has been decided. The next line is one sentence long and she is already gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note the deliberate parallel with the account of Zechariah just above, where an impossible birth is announced, questioned and confirmed with the same phrase. The surah was revealed to a community that included people familiar with the Christian account, and the sources report it being recited to a Christian court, so its careful wording about the child was heard by both audiences.

keyTerms.note: The same word given to Zechariah in this surah when he raised his own impossibility. Repeating it exactly links the two births and treats them as instances of one thing rather than as separate wonders.

A passive form from a root about completing a matter and passing judgement on it. It closes the exchange grammatically as well as in sense, since a settled matter is not one that discussion can reopen.
Distant in the sense of removed from where people are. Paired with the verb for withdrawing, it marks a second and deeper separation than the screen she had put up earlier in the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pregnancy could not be hidden for long in a settlement where women worked and washed together, and there was nowhere private to go for it. Travel alone was dangerous, and a woman without an escort on an open road was exposed to more than gossip. The single line that carries her from the announcement to a remote place covers a journey that would have been frightening at every stage.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names Jesus as the son of Mary more than twenty times, using the description as a title rather than only as an identification. He is the only figure in the Quran regularly named through his mother. The usage runs through both the Meccan and Medinan passages, and this surah, which carries her name, is where the fullest account of that relation is given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once and the tradition has held them together ever since. The birth is stated to be easy for God, which places it inside His power rather than outside the order of things, and the child is described as a sign and a mercy, which are terms the Quran uses of created things. The Quran holds Jesus in the highest honour among prophets while describing his origin in the same words it used for John's, a few lines earlier.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same phrase to Zechariah about the birth of John, earlier in this surah.
Answers her question in another surah with God creating what He wills by a word.
Describes her and her son together as a sign for all the worlds, in a single line.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk about a hardship you are carrying: whether it is entirely about you, or whether anyone else might be served by how you carry it. The announcement here does not tell Mary what she will gain. It tells her what her son will be for other people, and she is left to hold that on her own for a while.

studies.title: I Wish I Had Died
studies.meaning: The pains drive her to the trunk of a palm, and the verb used says she was forced there rather than that she chose it. Then the Quran records what she said, and it does not soften it. She wished she had died before this and been something forgotten, forgotten completely. Commentators are careful here. They read the wish as arising from what she was about to face among her people rather than from the pain, and they note that the Quran preserves the sentence of a woman it holds in the highest honour at the moment she could bear no more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that gives Mary's account at greater length than any other passage. The commentators describe her situation without embellishing it: alone, in labour, in an unsheltered place, and facing a return to a community that would draw the obvious conclusion. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It belongs to the narrative and is read within it.

keyTerms.note: A causative built on the verb for coming, so it means she was made to arrive there. The grammar removes her choice from the sentence, which is why the commentators read the palm as shelter reached under compulsion.
From a root about churning and violent movement. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the word carries the physical fact plainly rather than referring to it at a distance.

The passive participle repeats the noun it follows, an Arabic construction for absolute emphasis. She does not wish to be forgotten but to be a forgotten thing, twice over, with no trace left to be remembered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Birth in seventh-century Arabia happened among women. Mothers, aunts, neighbours and an experienced midwife attended, and their presence was the only medicine available. A woman giving birth alone in the open, without water prepared or hands to help, was in real danger and knew it. The palm trunk she reaches is not a comfort. It is the only thing in an empty place to hold on to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for labour pains in this ayah occurs only once in the whole Quran. The wish that follows it is also unusual: the Quran records people wishing themselves dead in only a few places, and most of them are said by the regretful on the Day of Judgement. This is the rare instance spoken by someone the text honours, in the middle of her life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to make a chosen servant of God into someone who does not suffer. Her words are preserved rather than corrected, and no rebuke follows them. What comes next is relief rather than reproach, which orders the two things clearly: the cry is answered, not judged. For a reader in real distress, the presence of this sentence in scripture, spoken by the woman the Quran honours most, does more than any consolation could.

crossReferences.why: Answers this cry immediately, with water, dates and an instruction to eat and be comforted.
Shows Jacob laying his grief and sorrow before God alone, without concealing its weight.
Records Jonah's call from the darkness, and the deliverance that answers it directly.

studies.applyIt: If you have ever said something like this in the worst hour of a bad week, notice that it is in the Quran, spoken by Mary. You do not have to be composed to be heard. The next time it rises in you, say it as a prayer rather than swallowing it, and then keep listening for what comes after.

studies.title: Shake The Palm Toward You
studies.meaning: The answer comes from below her, and the commentators differ over the caller, some reading the newborn and others the messenger who had come to her. First the grief is addressed: do not sorrow. Then two provisions, and they are arranged differently from each other. The stream is already there and requires nothing of her. The dates require her to take hold of a trunk and pull. Commentators note the pairing, since one gift is given outright and the other is given through an act she is barely able to perform.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators place the scene at a palm, and several describe it as dry or long dead, though the reports differ and the text does not say. What is agreed is the sequence: she had reached the end of what she could bear, and relief arrives immediately, in the form of water and food rather than of explanation.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sadness over something lost or feared, not for physical pain. What is addressed first is therefore her mind rather than her body, which is the order the passage keeps throughout.
The commentators record two readings: a rivulet of water running beneath her, or a person of high standing, meaning the child. Both are old, and the sources give the range rather than settling it.

Dates at the soft stage, before drying, when they are at their most nourishing and cannot be stored. The word occurs only here in the Quran, and it names the one form of the fruit that must be eaten at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fresh dates and water were exactly what a woman needed after birth, and every household in Arabia knew it. Dates were the staple that carried people through journeys and hunger, dense enough to restore someone quickly, and the soft ripe stage was the most prized and the most perishable. The provision here is not extraordinary food. It is the ordinary thing, arriving in a place where none of it should have been.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for soft ripe dates occurs only once in the whole Quran, in this ayah. The palm appears often in the text, in lists of what grows and in images of ruin, but the fruit at this particular stage, gathered and eaten fresh, is named a single time, at the moment it is dropped for a woman who has just given birth alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction to shake the trunk is doing something the tradition has long noticed. A woman at the limit of her strength is asked to make an effort that could not, by itself, bring down fruit. What follows is not proportional to what she does, and yet she is not spared the doing. Provision is arranged here so that it is unmistakably given and still requires a hand, which is how the Quran generally frames sustenance.

crossReferences.why: Continues the instruction: eat, drink, and be comforted, before she has to face anyone.
Describes provision reaching her before this, found with her whenever Zechariah entered.
States the principle at work here, provision arriving from where a person did not expect it.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are stuck, do the smallest available thing rather than the right-sized one. Send the one message, open the one file, walk to the end of the street. The instruction here is to pull at a trunk far too heavy to shake, and what follows is not produced by the pulling. It only begins with it.

studies.title: A Fast Of Silence
studies.meaning: Three instructions in one line, and the third is an idiom rather than a description: let your eye be cool, which in Arabic means let your worry settle. Then she is given something to say instead of an explanation. If anyone comes, tell them you have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful and will speak to no human today. Commentators note that the fast here is from speech rather than from food, since she has just been told to eat and drink, and that the instruction removes from her the burden of defending herself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Fasting from speech is described in the classical sources as a practice among earlier communities, and the commentators note it as belonging to their law rather than presenting it as a pattern for anyone after them. The surah gives Mary an answer to carry back before she has to face anybody, which is the shape of the whole passage: relief first, and then the return.

keyTerms.note: From the root for coolness. The Arabic idiom pairs it with the eye, since tears of grief were thought to run hot and tears of relief cool, so the phrase means to stop worrying rather than to feel joy.
The root means to hold back from something. This indefinite form occurs only once in the Quran, and the abstention meant here is from speech, since she has just been told to eat and drink.

A form built from the word for humankind, marking a single member of it. The choice of this word rather than the ordinary one keeps the restriction precise: she will not speak to any person, and nothing more is promised.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A vow was a serious public instrument. Someone who bound themselves to a fast, an offering or a silence was understood to be under an obligation that others should not interfere with, and pressing a person to break one was a real transgression. Mary is being given a sentence that would stop a crowd from questioning her, in a culture where the sentence carried actual weight and everybody present recognised it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a fast in this ayah occurs only once in the whole Quran. Everywhere else the Quran uses related forms, the verb or the plural, and this single indefinite noun appears here alone, describing not an abstention from food but from speaking to people, undertaken by a woman who had just been told to eat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction removes the need for self-defence at exactly the moment when defending herself would have been useless. What is given is not the argument that would win but the silence that makes an argument unnecessary, and the passage places the answering elsewhere. Vindication in this account does not come from Mary, and the structure of the scene means it could not have. Her part is to say one sentence and stop.

crossReferences.why: Gives Zechariah a silence too, three ayat into this surah, there as a sign rather than a shelter.
Shows what the silence makes room for, when she points and the answer comes from elsewhere.
Records the same restriction on speech given to Zechariah, with remembrance left open to him.

studies.applyIt: Next time you are accused of something unfairly, try saying one short true sentence and then stopping. Not a defence, not the full account, one sentence. Most of us keep talking because silence feels like agreement. This passage puts a woman in the worst version of that situation and gives her almost nothing to say.

studies.title: So She Pointed To Him
studies.meaning: She walks back carrying him, which the text states plainly, and the accusation arrives at once. What follows is worse than the charge: they invoke her family, naming her father's decency and her mother's, so the wrong is measured against people she loves. She answers by pointing. Commentators note that the gesture is the whole of her reply, and that the objection it draws is entirely reasonable. Nobody speaks with a child in the cradle. The scene is built so that her silence has no defence in it at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The address calling her sister of Aaron has been explained in several ways in the classical sources: that people were named after righteous figures of the past, that Aaron was a pious man of her own generation, or that she belonged to the priestly line descended from Aaron. The commentators record these readings side by side without ruling between them.

keyTerms.note: From a root about cutting or splitting something open. The word marks an act that tears through what is expected, so the accusation is not of an ordinary fault but of something without precedent.
The verb for indicating with a hand or a look rather than with words. It is the only thing she does in the scene, and it keeps the vow of silence she was told to declare in the previous ayah.
A place prepared and flattened for an infant, from a root about smoothing ground. The Quran uses the same word for the earth itself, laid out level for the people who live on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An accusation of this kind was not a private matter. It touched a whole household, since a family's standing was collective, and the two people named here were the ones who would carry the shame with her for the rest of their lives. Naming a person's parents in a public reproach was the standard way of making a charge land hardest. It said that the offence was not only against her own name but against theirs.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a cradle appears four times in the Quran. Three of them are about this child speaking from it, once here and twice in another surah where it is announced in advance that he will do so. The fourth is about the earth itself, described as a cradle spread out and made level for the people who live on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage arranges vindication so that it cannot be claimed by the person vindicated. She points, and what answers is not her word but something outside her entirely. That protects the account from becoming a story about a woman clever enough to escape a charge, and it makes her innocence a matter of what God does rather than what she manages. The reader is also given the crowd's objection in full, which the Quran often does when the reply is about to make it irrelevant.

crossReferences.why: Announces before his birth that he will speak to people from the cradle and in maturity.
Names the accusation against Mary directly as a grave falsehood spoken against her.
Describes her chastity and makes her and her son together a sign for all the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you were misjudged and how much energy went into explaining. Pick one small misunderstanding you are still carrying and decide, deliberately, to leave it unexplained for a month. Not every one, just this one. Notice how much of the discomfort was about the accusation and how much was about not being able to answer it.

studies.title: I Am The Servant Of God
studies.meaning: The first words are a self-description, and they begin at the lowest point rather than the highest: servant of God. Only after that come the Scripture and the prophethood. What follows is a list of what has been done to him and enjoined on him, all in the passive or with God as the actor, so nothing is claimed. Blessed wherever he is, charged with prayer and giving as long as he lives, made kind to his mother. Commentators note that the mother is named where a father would ordinarily be, and that the answer to the accusation is entirely indirect.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report this surah being recited before the Christian ruler of Abyssinia when Muslims sought protection at his court, and this passage is at the heart of what would have been heard there. The Quran's account of Jesus was of immediate practical importance to the early community, since it defined both what they shared with Christians and where they differed.

keyTerms.note: The word for one who belongs entirely to another. Placing it first, before Scripture or prophethood, sets the relation that everything after it is arranged inside, and the Quran uses the same title for its highest figures.
From a root about a camel kneeling and settling in a place, hence something that stays and increases where it rests. Blessing in Arabic is durable good rather than a moment of luck.
Specifically the woman who gave birth, not the general word for a parent. In a scene where his mother is being accused, the word chosen is the one that names exactly the relation in question.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person in that world was placed by their father's name, and a child introduced without one had no social location at all. The formula was fixed: so-and-so, son of so-and-so, of such a clan. To hear a speech of self-introduction that names a mother and no father would have been arresting to any Arabian listener, and it is exactly the gap the crowd in this passage had just been pointing at.
studies.didYouKnow: The list of qualities given here runs closely parallel to the list given a few ayat earlier for John: both are told to hold the Scripture or given it, both are described as kind to a parent, and both are said not to have been made overbearing. The surah describes the two cousins in nearly matching terms, and the differences between the two lists are as deliberate as the likenesses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the words is the theology. Servanthood comes first, and everything else is described as given rather than possessed, which is the position the Quran maintains about Jesus throughout. The passage also does something for the reader about honour. The highest thing said of a human being in this text is not that he was raised above the condition of a servant but that he filled it completely, and the same title is used of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at the opening of the previous surah.

crossReferences.why: Gives the closely matching list for John a few ayat earlier, in the same surah.
States that he would never disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the nearest angels.
Describes him as a servant on whom God bestowed favour, made an example for the Children of Israel.

studies.applyIt: Write down how you would introduce yourself to someone who does not know you. Look at what comes first: work, family, where you are from, something you have achieved. Then notice what comes first in this speech. You do not have to change your answer. It is worth knowing what you actually lead with.

studies.title: The Word Of Truth
studies.meaning: The speech closes with peace pronounced over three moments, birth, death and being raised alive, and it is said in the first person, where the same formula earlier in this surah was said about John by God. Then the narration steps back and names him: that is Jesus, son of Mary. The phrase that follows calls this the statement of truth about which they are in doubt. Commentators note that the surah has given his own words first and only then supplied the identification, so the description comes after the testimony rather than before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Christian communities were present in Arabia, at Najran in the south and along the trade routes north, and Christian doctrine about the person of Jesus had been the subject of long and serious debate within those communities for centuries. The Quran addresses that setting directly, and the classical sources report this surah being recited at a Christian court, where these ayat would have been heard by people who held a different view.

keyTerms.note: Definite here, where the same formula spoken over John a few ayat earlier is indefinite. Commentators read the difference as him invoking the peace already established rather than pronouncing a new one.

The plain word for something said. Used with the word for truth it makes a claim about accuracy of report, and the commentators read it as describing the account just given rather than as a title for him.

keyTerms.gloss: they are in doubt, they dispute
keyTerms.note: A form carrying both uncertainty and argument with others about it. It occurs twice in the Quran, and it describes a disagreement being carried on rather than a settled position anybody holds quietly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Questions about the person of Jesus were live and consequential in the region. Churches in Syria, Egypt and Abyssinia had divided over them, councils had met, and communities defined themselves by the answers they gave. Arabian traders travelling north or to Abyssinia encountered these communities and their disagreements, so the reference here to people in dispute described something the first audience could observe rather than something they were told about.
studies.didYouKnow: The threefold peace appears twice in this surah, over John and over Jesus, in almost identical words. The difference is who speaks it. Over John it is pronounced in the narration, in the third person; here it is spoken by Jesus himself in the first person. Two accounts placed side by side, with the same blessing arriving from two directions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran holds Jesus in the highest honour, as a prophet, a sign and a mercy, and it also states that he is the son of Mary and a servant of God. Christians have understood his person differently, and that difference is not small; the ayah names it as a matter people dispute rather than pretending it away. What this passage offers as its own answer is the speech just given, in which he describes himself. Readers are left with testimony.

crossReferences.why: Pronounces the same threefold peace over John, earlier in this surah, in the third person.
Compares his creation to Adam's, both made by God's word without an ordinary origin.
Records him questioned on the Day and answering that he said only what he was commanded.

studies.applyIt: If you know someone whose faith differs from yours on something central, read this passage and notice how it works: the account is given, the disagreement is named honestly, and nothing is smoothed over. Try that shape in one conversation this week. Say what you hold, say where you differ, and do not pretend the difference is smaller than it is.

studies.title: He Says Be And It Is
studies.meaning: The statement is put as a matter of what is fitting rather than of what is possible, which is a particular way of speaking. Taking a child is not something that belongs to God, and the declaration of His transcendence follows immediately. Then a reason is supplied from another direction entirely. When He decrees a matter He says to it be, and it is. Commentators note the logic: offspring is how a limited being continues itself, and a will that produces by command has no need of continuation at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah addresses more than one audience at once. Some Arabs described the angels as daughters of God, which the Quran answers repeatedly in the Meccan surahs, and Christian communities in and around Arabia held a doctrine about the sonship of Christ that they had worked out over centuries. The commentators note both settings and do not collapse them into each other.

keyTerms.note: A verb of acquiring something for oneself, used in Arabic for adopting a son rather than fathering one. Negated with the construction that opens the ayah, it denies that such an act befits God at all.

The verb for bringing a matter to completion and passing final judgement on it. Used of God it names a decision that is already finished, which is why the sentence that follows describes an outcome rather than a process.

The imperative of the plainest verb in the language, two letters long. The Quran uses this construction in eight places, always for creation without means, and it is deliberately the shortest possible way to say it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the organising fact of Arabian life. A man's sons carried his name, held his property, avenged him and kept him from disappearing, and to die without them was the worst outcome available. Sonship was how anything continued at all. That is exactly what the ayah is answering: it denies of God the one mechanism by which everything in that world secured a future for itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The command that creates, two letters in Arabic, appears in eight places across the Quran. Two of them are about the creation of Jesus specifically, one answering Mary's own question about how she could have a son, and one comparing his origin to Adam's. The same brief phrase covers the making of the heavens and the earth and the making of one child.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument turns on how creation works rather than on the status of any particular figure. If bringing something into being takes only a word, then generation, which is the transmission of a nature from one being to another, is not the category involved. That is why the Quran can affirm the miraculous birth in the strongest terms while denying sonship, and why the commentators treat the two halves of this ayah as a single argument rather than as a denial followed by an unrelated statement.

crossReferences.why: Compares his creation to Adam's, made from dust and told to be, then he was.
States the same denial in the shortest surah of its kind, alongside the denial of any equal.
Asks how He could have a child when there is no consort, and He created everything.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you plan assumes that things take time and material: money first, then the move; health first, then the change. Some of that is simply prudence. But spend a minute today with the idea that the outcome you are managing toward does not need your materials to arrive, and see whether your grip loosens at all.

studies.title: My Lord And Your Lord
studies.meaning: The passage gives what is presented as the plain instruction, and it is one sentence: God is my Lord and yours, so worship Him, and this is a straight path. Nothing complicated is being asked. The next line reports what happened to it. Parties differed among themselves, and the disagreement is described as arising after the instruction rather than instead of it. Commentators read the ayat as marking the distance between a teaching and the history that follows it, which is a pattern the Quran describes for more than one community.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Christian communities of the region had spent centuries in serious and often painful disagreement over the person of Christ, with councils, divisions and separate churches resulting. The Quran refers to that history as something its first audience could observe along the trade routes. The commentators note the word for the differing parties is one the Quran uses of groups within earlier communities generally, not of one church against another.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for servant used at the start of this speech. The instruction and the speaker's self-description share a root, so what he asks of others is what he has just called himself.

Groups formed around a position, from a root about banding together. The Quran uses it of divisions within earlier communities and of alliances formed against a messenger, and both senses involve people organised into sides.
The place or moment where something is witnessed. Applied to the Day it names the event as something attended and seen, which is why the ayah that follows speaks of hearing and sight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian traders travelling north to Syria or south to Yemen passed through territory where Christian communities held different positions and knew it about each other. Abyssinia across the sea held another. Meccans dealt with all of them commercially and would have known that people who revered the same figure had separated over how to describe him. The reference in this ayah was to something within the audience's own experience of the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The long section of this surah that runs to this point rhymes on one sound almost without a break, thirty-two ayat in a row. At exactly the passage that turns to the disagreement about Jesus, the rhyme changes, and it stays changed for seven ayat before returning. The shift in subject and the shift in sound begin and end together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction quoted here is the common ground, and the Quran states it in a form that a monotheist of any of these communities would recognise. What follows is not an argument but an observation about time: teachings are given plainly and then contested by those who inherit them. The passage therefore locates the problem in what happened after rather than in what was said, which is why the reply to disagreement here is a warning about a Day rather than a refutation.

crossReferences.why: Has him say he told them only this, to worship God, his Lord and theirs.
Repeats the same sentence and reports the same differing among parties immediately afterwards.
Describes communities dividing only after knowledge came to them, out of rivalry among themselves.

studies.applyIt: Find the simplest true sentence about your own faith, the one you would say if you had five words. Say it to yourself before you pray this week rather than working through anything longer. Most disagreement grows in the elaboration, and it is worth knowing what remains when the elaboration is set aside.

studies.title: The Day Of Regret
studies.meaning: A day is named by the feeling it produces, which the Quran rarely does. The matter is concluded, and the naming turns on the moment after a decision when nothing further can be done about it. The present state of the people is given in the same breath: heedless and not believing, which is what makes the regret possible. Then ownership is stated. We inherit the earth and everyone on it. Commentators note the word chosen, since inheriting is what happens when the previous holders are gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been recounting how earlier communities divided after their teachings were given, and the warning here follows directly from that. The commentators do not report an occasion for these ayat. The instruction to mention Abraham at the end of the passage begins the surah's second long sequence, which runs through several prophets in turn.

keyTerms.note: From a root about stripping something bare or wearing it out, so the sorrow of someone left exposed with nothing to show. The phrase naming a Day by this word occurs only here in the Quran.

Not ignorance but the state of having something in front of you and not registering it. The word implies the information was available, which is why it is the condition that makes later regret possible.
The verb for receiving what is left when a holder has gone. Used of God and the earth it says nothing about acquisition and everything about who remains when every present owner has finished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance was the most watched event in an Arabian family. Herds, wells, houses and debts changed hands at a death, and disputes over them could split a clan for a generation. Everyone in the audience had seen property pass out of hands that had held it for decades. The ayah takes that ordinary and slightly grim process and applies it to the earth itself, with one holder left at the end.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names the Day of Judgement by many titles, and most of them describe the event: the Day of Rising, the Day of Reckoning, the Day of Separation. This is the only place it is named for what people will feel on it. The phrase occurs once in the whole text, and the word behind it means the grief of someone left with nothing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming a day for regret rather than for judgement puts the reader inside the experience rather than in front of a verdict. That is a specific move, and the ayat that follow explain why it works: the people described are not opposed, only inattentive, and inattention is the condition most readers will recognise in themselves. The statement about inheritance then removes the assumption underneath the heedlessness, which is that what a person holds is theirs to keep.

crossReferences.why: States the same diagnosis directly: their reckoning has drawn near while they turn away heedless.
Repeats that it is We who give life and cause death, and We who are the inheritors.
Quotes the regret itself, spoken too late over what was neglected toward God.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you would regret not having done if this year were the last one. Do not make a plan for it. Just take the first ten minutes of it this week: the phone call, the appointment, the apology. Regret in this ayah is about a moment when the doing is no longer available, and ten minutes is usually enough to move something out of that category.

studies.title: Why Do You Worship That
studies.meaning: The first thing recorded of Abraham in this surah is not a declaration but a question put to his father, and the form of address is the tender one a child uses. The question itself is practical rather than theological. What you serve does not hear, does not see, and is of no use to you. Commentators note that he begins where his father already agrees, since nobody claimed the carved figures could hear, and that the argument works by drawing out an implication his father had never applied.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the account had immediate force for the first audience. Abraham was claimed as an ancestor by the Arabs of Mecca and honoured as the builder of the sanctuary, and the objects around that sanctuary were the ones his own argument had been directed against. The commentators note that the Quran tells this story to people who traced their lineage to him while practising what he had left.

keyTerms.note: An affectionate vocative, softer than the plain word for father. Arabic grammarians describe the ending as standing in for a possessive of endearment, so the address carries warmth into an argument about something serious.
A short interrogative asking for a reason. It opens the whole exchange as a question rather than a statement, which puts the burden of the answer on the person addressed rather than on the speaker.

From the root behind wealth and sufficiency, so the verb means to meet a need or make someone independent of it. The question is therefore about usefulness, which is the ground his father would have accepted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Household images were ordinary property. A family kept them, inherited them and could name which ancestor had acquired which one, and their manufacture was a trade in itself. Nobody supposed the wood or stone had ears. They were held to be representations of something that did, or to carry standing by association. Abraham's question does not attack a belief anybody stated aloud; it presses on what everyone would have conceded if asked.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham addresses his father as my father four times in this passage, once at the start of each of four consecutive ayat. The Quran uses that affectionate form of address eight times in all, so half of its occurrences in the entire text fall inside these four ayat, spoken by one son in one conversation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models an argument that begins with a shared premise rather than with a claim, and that keeps the relationship intact while making it. The Quran preserves the tenderness of the address across a conversation that ends in rejection and separation, which says something about how disagreement with those closest to us can be conducted. It also frames worship as a question about what actually answers, which is the same test the Quran applies elsewhere to anything invoked.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same challenge to his people, ending with him naming the Lord of the heavens and earth.
Records the same question at greater length, with the answer that they found their fathers doing so.
Names the exchange with his father directly and states that he saw them in clear error.

studies.applyIt: Pick a disagreement you have with someone in your family and try starting from what you both already accept, rather than from where you differ. One question, asked kindly, about something they would not dispute. The form of address in this passage does as much work as the argument, and it is the part most of us drop first.

studies.title: Follow Me To A Level Way
studies.meaning: The son says something that reverses the order of a household, and the way he says it is the whole difficulty. Knowledge has come to me that did not come to you, so follow me. Commentators note the careful phrasing: the knowledge is described as having arrived, not as having been acquired, so no superiority is claimed for the person, only a difference in what reached him. The offer that follows is guidance to a path that is level, and it is put as an invitation rather than as an instruction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources place Abraham in a society where religious practice was inherited and a father's position on it settled the household's. The commentators note that the demand being made here, that a father follow his son, would have been socially extraordinary in that world and in the Arabia of the first audience, where families that accepted the message faced exactly this reversal.

keyTerms.note: The verb of arrival, with the knowledge as its subject and him as its destination. He is described as the place it reached rather than the person who found it, which removes any claim of merit from the sentence.
The verb for walking behind someone on a road. It is a request to be led rather than to be believed, which is why the clause that follows describes a way rather than a set of statements.
Ground that is flat and free of obstacles, from a root about being properly formed. A level way is not merely correct but walkable, which is what he is offering rather than a proof.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in Arabia were graded by whether they could be walked. A level track meant a route without ravines, loose rock or climbs that broke a camel's pace, and travellers chose longer level ways over shorter rough ones without hesitation. Guidance was a practical service, offered by people who had made the journey. To offer a level way was to offer something a traveller could take with a full load.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a level way here is the same word used earlier in this surah for a body in sound working order, when Zechariah is told he will not speak for three nights while remaining whole, and again when the messenger appears to Mary in well-made human form. The surah uses one word for an intact body and an unbroken road.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the possession of knowledge from any claim about the person holding it, which matters for how a believer speaks to anyone. Nothing here says the son is wiser or better; it says something reached him. That leaves the father's dignity intact while the request is made, and it locates authority in what was given rather than in who received it. The invitation is also framed as movement rather than assent, so what is asked for is a step.

crossReferences.why: Opens the same conversation with a question rather than a claim, in the ayah just before.
Sets out how to treat parents who press a different way: keep company with them well.
Describes calling to God upon insight, by the messenger and by those who follow him.

studies.applyIt: If you know something someone close to you does not, and it matters, try saying it the way this ayah does. Not I understand this better than you, but this came to me. It is a small difference in wording and it changes what the other person has to defend. Use it once this week.

studies.title: I Fear For You
studies.meaning: The address stays tender while the content sharpens. Do not serve the tempter, who was disobedient to the Most Merciful, and then the reason is given in the first person as fear rather than as judgement. I am afraid a punishment will touch you. Commentators note that the son does not say his father is condemned; he says what he is afraid of, and the difference is the whole tone of the passage. The last word describes what would follow, an alliance with the one he had just been warned against.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the parallel to the first audience was direct. Muslims in Mecca were watching family members refuse the message, and several classical reports describe believers pleading with parents and relatives without effect. The commentators read this sequence as a model for that situation, since it shows a conversation carried as far as it can be carried and then ending without either the affection or the position being abandoned.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so not a single refusal but a settled disposition. The same word closes the description of John earlier in this surah, where he is said not to have been made overbearing and disobedient.

The plain verb of fear, in the first person. It makes the warning a report of the speaker's own state rather than a verdict on the person addressed, which is why the ayah does not read as a condemnation.

The word for someone bound to you by protection and loyalty. Earlier in this surah Zechariah asks for one as an heir, so the same term names both the answer to a prayer and the outcome being feared here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliance in Arabia was the whole architecture of safety. A person without a protector could be killed with impunity, and the bond was entered publicly and taken seriously by everybody. The final word of this passage uses that vocabulary. It does not describe his father becoming wicked; it describes him ending up under the protection of the wrong party, which was the most concrete way of naming a disaster in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a close ally occurs twice in this surah, and the two uses stand at opposite ends of what a person can hope for. Zechariah asks God for one at the surah's opening, meaning an heir to carry his trust after him. Here Abraham names the same relation as the thing he most fears his father will fall into.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates warning from condemnation, which is difficult to do and easy to lose. Everything is stated as the speaker's fear rather than as the listener's fate, so the outcome is left where the Quran usually leaves it, with God. The affectionate address across all four ayat carries a second point. Disagreement about the most serious matter available does not license contempt, and the tenderness in this conversation is not softening but the form the argument takes.

crossReferences.why: Gives the father's answer and the son's reply, where he leaves while still promising to pray for him.
Sets a counsel to a son beside an instruction to accompany parents well even in disagreement.
Records Abraham's example, including the promise made to his father and its limit.

studies.applyIt: If you are worried about someone you love and cannot reach them, try changing one sentence: from what they are doing wrong to what you are afraid of. Say it once, plainly, and then let it rest. This passage is the record of a conversation that did not succeed and stayed loving anyway, which is more useful than one that worked.

studies.title: Peace Be Upon You
studies.meaning: The father answers, and the tenderness is entirely on one side now. He asks whether his son is turning away from his gods, threatens to stone him, and tells him to leave for a long while. The reply is three short clauses and none of them argues. Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; He has always been gracious to me. Commentators note that the last clause explains the second. He asks forgiveness for a man who has just threatened to kill him because he has himself been treated generously.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and directly relevant to the first audience. Believers in Mecca were being disowned, threatened and in some cases physically attacked by their own families, and the classical sources describe individuals cut off entirely by fathers and uncles. The commentators read the promise of forgiveness here alongside later ayat that set a limit to it, and note that the Quran preserves both the promise and its limit.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic form, so a stated intention rather than an outburst. Stoning was a means of killing that spread responsibility across a crowd, which is part of why the threat carried weight in a small community.
A stretch of time, from a root about fullness and duration. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it makes the dismissal open-ended rather than a demand to go away for the evening.
One who receives another warmly and takes trouble over them. It occurs only here, and it names the manner of God's dealing with him, which is offered as the reason he can answer a threat this way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being told to leave was not an inconvenience in that world. A person outside their family's protection had no standing, no shelter and no one to answer for them, and the roads were dangerous to anyone travelling without a name behind them. The father is not throwing a young man out of a house. He is removing the only thing keeping him alive, and both of them understand that.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words in these two ayat occur nowhere else in the Quran: the one describing how long the father wants him gone, and the one describing how God has dealt with the son. A single exchange carries two words the text never uses again, one at the end of the threat and one at the end of the reply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply models a response that neither concedes nor retaliates. Peace is offered, forgiveness is sought for the other party, and the position is not withdrawn, since the next ayah continues the separation. That combination is hard to hold and the passage does not present it as easy. The reason given is also worth noting: he does not appeal to his own patience but to how he has been treated, so his generosity is described as something passed on rather than produced.

crossReferences.why: Cites this same promise of forgiveness as an example, while marking where the example stops.
Explains that the asking of forgiveness was due to a promise, and states when it ended.
Describes the servants of the Most Merciful answering the ignorant with a word of peace.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who has treated you badly and, without contacting them, ask God to forgive them once. Do not tell anybody you did it and do not expect it to change how you feel. This ayah puts the request immediately after a death threat, which suggests the point is not that the feeling has resolved first.

studies.title: Perhaps I Will Not Be Wretched
studies.meaning: He states what he will do rather than what they should. I withdraw from you and from what you call on besides God, and I will call on my Lord. The two halves use the same verb, so the sentence turns on what a person calls to. The last clause is the surprising one. He says perhaps he will not be disappointed in calling his Lord, which stops short of certainty. Commentators note the humility of the phrasing: a man leaving everything for God does not claim the outcome, he hopes for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The parallel to the first audience was immediate, since Muslims in Mecca were separating from families and from a shrine that was the centre of their city's life. The commentators note that this ayah describes a departure that is stated in advance and carried out in the next line, and that what follows it is a gift rather than a hardship.

keyTerms.note: A verb for setting oneself apart from a group, not for hostility toward it. It describes leaving a company rather than opposing it, which fits the peace he had offered a line earlier.
The same verb used for what they call on besides God, repeated in the same sentence. Arabic sets the two invocations side by side using one word, so the difference is entirely in the object.
One left in misery, from a root about hardship and toil that yields nothing. Denying it of his own calling means hoping the effort will not come back empty, which is the fear behind any prayer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: To withdraw from your people in Arabia was to become a stranger, and strangers had no rights that anyone was obliged to honour. Water at a well, passage across territory, help when ill, all of it ran through belonging. A man announcing that he would separate himself was describing a future of real exposure. The hope in the last clause of this ayah is being expressed by someone who has just given up every ordinary security.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah begins with a call made in secret, by Zechariah, and answered. Here, near its middle, Abraham makes a call while leaving everything behind, and expresses only a hope that it will not be wasted. Both men use the same root for calling on God, and in both cases the surah reports the answer in the ayah immediately following.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The hesitation in the closing clause is the theological point. He does not treat God as obliged, even while doing the hardest thing available for God's sake, and the Quran preserves that hesitation rather than replacing it with confidence. Prayer here is an act of hope rather than a claim of entitlement. What follows in the next ayah then answers it beyond what was asked, which is how the surah has been arranging every request it records.

crossReferences.why: Answers this immediately, granting him sons and prophethood after the withdrawal is carried out.
Shows the same pattern at the surah's opening: a call made, and answered beyond the request.
States the standing invitation, that God will respond to those who call on Him.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something this week without deciding in advance what the answer means about you. If it comes, it was given; if it does not, the asking was still the right thing. Abraham says only that he hopes he will not be disappointed, and that phrasing is worth borrowing on the days when a request matters a lot.

studies.title: When He Left Them
