studies.meaning: The withdrawal announced in the previous ayah is carried out, and the sentence reports it in the same words he had used, so nothing was said that was not done. What follows is the reply, and it does not answer the request he made. He had asked for nothing except not to be disappointed; he is given a son and a grandson, and both are made prophets. Commentators note that a man who had just lost a father is given a family, and that the loss and the gift are placed in one sentence with nothing between them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Abraham left his homeland and travelled west, and the Quran assumes the outline of that journey without narrating it. The commentators note that this ayah passes over the whole of it and joins the departure directly to the outcome. For an audience in Mecca watching people leave families for the message, and shortly before some of them would leave the city itself, the compression was the point.

keyTerms.note: The same verb he had used of himself a line earlier, now reported in the narration. Repeating it exactly is how the Quran often marks a stated intention being carried through without alteration.
The verb for giving something outright, with no return expected and no prior claim on it. The Quran uses it especially for children, and it appears three times in this stretch of the surah.

A word marking that what follows applies to both individually rather than jointly. The prophethood is therefore said of each of them separately, which is why the sentence does not simply say a line of prophets.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your people meant leaving your future as well as your past. Marriages were arranged inside a network of kin, and a man outside it had no obvious way to form a household at all. Descendants were the only continuity anyone had. The answer given here is precisely the thing his departure should have cost him, and an audience in seventh-century Arabia would have felt the shape of that immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for granting outright occurs three times in a few consecutive ayat of this surah. Here it grants Abraham a son and a grandson; a line later it grants their family mercy and a reputation of truth; and a line after that it grants Moses his brother Aaron. The same word gives children, standing and a companion in three consecutive gifts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah establishes an order the Quran uses repeatedly: the leaving comes first and the provision follows, and the provision is not the thing that was asked for. That keeps the departure from being a transaction, since he did not know what was coming, and it keeps the gift from being a payment. What he receives also answers the specific loss he took, which the passage states without commenting on it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same emigration and the same grant of Isaac and Jacob, with prophethood in his line.
Describes his deliverance to a blessed land and the gift of Jacob as something additional.
Has him say he is going to his Lord who will guide him, and ask for a righteous son.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you gave up for a reason you still believe in, and which cost you more than you expected. Do not try to find the compensation for it. Just write down what you actually received in the years afterwards, whether or not it looks connected. The ayah puts the leaving and the gift in one sentence, without explaining the join.

studies.title: Called From The Right Side
studies.meaning: The family is given mercy and something the Arabic calls a high tongue of truth, meaning a name spoken well of by those who come after. Then the surah turns to Moses with three descriptions and no narrative: chosen and made pure, a messenger, a prophet. What follows is the one scene it gives him, and it is not a plague or a sea. He was called from the right side of the mountain and brought near in private conversation. Commentators note the choice. The event singled out is an intimacy rather than a wonder.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is moving through a sequence of prophets, and the commentators note that each is introduced with the same instruction to mention them in the Book, followed by a short description rather than a story. The account of Moses at the mountain is told at length in other surahs; here it is reduced to the moment of being called and brought close, which fits the chapter's concern with what passes privately between God and a person.

keyTerms.note: Arabic uses the word for tongue to mean what people say about someone. Paired with truth it names a good name that is also deserved, which is why the phrase describes reputation and accuracy at once.
A passive form, so someone purified by God rather than someone who purified himself. The Quran uses it of those set apart for God, and the passive is what distinguishes it from ordinary sincerity.
From a root about private talk between two parties. It occurs twice in the Quran, once of brothers withdrawing to confer among themselves and once here, of a man brought near to speak with God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to a chief was staged. You waited, you were announced, you spoke at a distance in front of others, and being called forward to speak privately was the highest mark of favour a person could receive. Everyone in the audience understood the difference between being addressed in an assembly and being drawn aside. The word this ayah uses for the mountain scene is the word for that second thing.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing the good name given to Abraham's family appears twice in the Quran. In the other place, Abraham himself is praying, asking his Lord to grant him exactly this, a tongue of truth among later generations. Here it is reported as granted. The request and its answer are recorded in two different surahs, in the same words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the mountain as a private conversation rather than as a commissioning changes what the reader takes from it. Prophethood is presented in this surah as proximity before it is presented as function, and the same emphasis runs through the chapter's other accounts, which favour what happened between a person and God over what they achieved among people. The good name given to Abraham's line also makes a point about reputation: it is described as granted rather than built.

crossReferences.why: Records Abraham praying for exactly this good name among later generations, in his own words.
Gives the scene at the mountain at length, with the call, the fire and the instruction.
States that God spoke to Moses directly, the distinction this passage records in one word.

studies.applyIt: Think about which you would rather have: to be known for something, or to have one honest conversation with someone who matters. Most of us say the second and arrange our week around the first. Take twenty minutes this week for the second kind, with God or with a person, and notice what you had to move to make room.

studies.title: True To His Promise
studies.meaning: A brother is described as a gift out of mercy, which is an unusual way to speak of a sibling. Then Ishmael is introduced, and the first thing said of him is that he was true to what he promised. Commentators note the phrase is used of him alone in the Quran. What follows is domestic rather than public: he used to instruct his own household in prayer and giving, and he was pleasing to his Lord. A prophet's record here is his family and his word, in that order.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the naming of Ishmael carried particular weight in that city. The Arabs of the region traced their descent to him, and the sanctuary at Mecca was associated with him and his father. The commentators note that the Quran presents him to that audience not through lineage or through the sanctuary but through keeping his word and teaching his household, which was a pointed way of introducing an ancestor everyone claimed.

keyTerms.note: The active participle of truthfulness, joined here to the word for a promise. The construction makes truthfulness his standing quality with respect to what he undertook, rather than an act he performed once.
What a person binds themselves to do. The Quran uses the same word for God's own promises, so describing a man as true to his is a considerable thing to say of him.
A passive form, so approved of by another rather than pleased in himself. Placed at the end of a description that is entirely domestic, it attaches God's approval to what he did inside his own house.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise was the only enforcement mechanism Arabia had. There were no courts and almost no written contracts, so trade credit, safe passage, marriage arrangements and truces all rested on whether a man was known to keep his word. Someone who broke a promise was not fined; he was simply never trusted again, and neither was his family. Being called true to his promise was the highest commercial and social character reference available.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing Ishmael as true to his promise occurs only once in the whole Quran, and it is said of no one else. The Quran names several prophets by a single defining quality in this surah, and this is the one it gives him, in a passage otherwise concerned with prayer, giving and his own household.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The description locates a prophet's worth in kept promises and in a household taught, rather than in a following or a conquest. That is a deliberate reordering. It also joins two things the reader may keep apart: reliability with people and standing with God, since the ayah moves directly from instructing his family to being approved by his Lord, with no transition. What is done at home is presented as the record, not the preparation for one.

crossReferences.why: Shows him accepting what he was told and promising to be found patient, if God wills.
Gives the same instruction to the Prophet: enjoin prayer on your family and be steadfast in it.
Places him with his father raising the foundations of the House, asking for it to be accepted.

studies.applyIt: Look at the last three things you said you would do for someone and check whether you did them. Not the large commitments, the small ones: the message you would send, the thing you would look up. Pick one that is outstanding and close it today. The description in this ayah is of a man whose word could be relied on in ordinary matters.

studies.title: Raised To A High Place
studies.meaning: Two ayat and almost nothing in them. He is named, described as a man of truth and a prophet, and then raised to a high place. Commentators differ over what the raising means, some reading an elevation of rank and others a physical raising, and they record the disagreement without resolving it. The Quran gives no story, no people, no message and no outcome. What the reader is given is a name held in the same list as Abraham and Moses, and one sentence about where he was placed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Idris is named only twice in the Quran, here and in a short list in another surah, and the classical sources have long discussed who he is, with a number of identifications proposed and none of them settled. The commentators generally note the limits of what is known rather than filling the gap, which is why the passage is usually read as it stands.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the word for truthful, describing someone whose truthfulness is habitual rather than occasional. This exact form occurs twice in the Quran, both in this surah, of him and of Abraham.
The plain verb for lifting something up. Its ordinariness is what leaves the commentators divided, since Arabic uses it for physical raising and for elevation in rank with equal frequency.
An adjective of height, and one of the names of God in its definite form. Used here of a place, it says the position is high without saying where it is or what it consists of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian audiences knew far more names than stories. Genealogies ran for dozens of generations and were recited accurately, but most of those names carried no narrative at all, only a reputation attached to them. A figure honoured without an account was a familiar thing rather than a puzzle. Hearing a name placed in a list of the greatest, with one line about him, would have been how most of the past reached them.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive word for truthfulness used of him occurs twice in the Quran in this exact form, and both are in this surah. The other is used of Abraham, fifteen ayat earlier, in a sentence built the same way. The chapter gives its two most compressed prophetic portraits the same opening description.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows the Quran declining to fill a gap. A figure is honoured, and almost nothing is disclosed about him, which sets a limit the tradition has generally respected. That has a practical effect on how the past is treated: what is given is enough to establish that God has raised people the reader knows nothing about. It also implies something about the record itself, since the honour here does not depend on anyone remembering why.

crossReferences.why: Names him again in a short list, describing all of them as patient and admitted into mercy.
Uses the same intensive word for truthfulness of Abraham, earlier in this surah.
States that messengers were sent whose accounts have not been related at all.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who did something good that nobody recorded: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbour who kept a family going. Say their name once today and ask God to raise them. The passage honours a man whose story was not preserved, which suggests that being remembered by people is not the thing that fixes a person's standing.

studies.title: They Fell Down Weeping
studies.meaning: The whole sequence of prophets is gathered into one sentence and traced through four lines of descent, from Adam, from those carried with Noah, from Abraham's line and from Israel's, and then a fifth category that is not descent at all: those God guided and chose. Commentators note that the list ends by breaking its own pattern. What follows is not what they taught but what they did when revelation was recited: they went down prostrating and weeping. The people at the top of the list are described by their response.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has moved through Zechariah, John, Mary, Jesus, Abraham, Moses, Aaron, Ishmael and Idris, each introduced with the same instruction to mention them in the Book. This ayah closes that sequence and gathers it. The commentators read the four lines of descent as covering the prophets named above in order, which is why the list runs from the earliest to the latest.

keyTerms.note: The verb behind the word for a blessing received. It makes prophethood something done to these figures rather than achieved by them, which is the grammar the whole ayah keeps.
From a root about gathering something up and picking it out for oneself. It names a choosing that is not based on lineage, which is why it stands last, after four lines of descent have been given.
A plural form describing many people in tears at once. Paired with prostration it makes the response bodily and shared, and it is the last word of the ayah before the recitation mark.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was how the past was held. A man could recite his ancestors for many generations and place any stranger by asking two questions, and the whole social order rested on those lines. This ayah uses that structure, listing prophets by descent exactly as an Arabian audience would have expected, and then adds a category that has no lineage in it at all, which would have been the arresting part.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the ayat at which the reciter and listeners traditionally prostrate, and the printed text carries a small mark at the end of it. There are fourteen or fifteen such places in the Quran, depending on the tradition of recitation followed. This one falls at the end of an ayah that describes prophets falling down in exactly that way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Adding a category of the guided and chosen after four genealogies opens the list beyond descent, which matters for every reader who is not in any of those lines. The closing description then sets the standard, and it is not scholarship or authority but response. The greatest figures in the chapter are characterised by what happened to them when they heard revelation, which places the reader in the same position as them at the moment of reading.

crossReferences.why: Asks for the path of those God has favoured, using the same verb as this ayah.
Describes the same response, falling on their faces weeping, in the surah just before this one.
Shows eyes overflowing at hearing the revelation, in people who recognised what they heard.

studies.applyIt: Read this ayah aloud to the end and stop at the mark. Notice that the tradition of pausing here grows out of the ayah's own last words, which describe people going down and weeping. Then read it once more and ask which part of you responded, if any. The chapter measures its greatest figures by their response rather than their record.

studies.title: Except Whoever Turns Back
studies.meaning: A generation follows the one just praised, and two things are said of it: they let the prayer go and they followed their appetites. Commentators are careful about the first verb, which means to lose or waste rather than to abandon outright, and read it as neglecting the prayer or emptying it out rather than announcing its end. Then the exception arrives before the sentence has time to settle. Whoever turns back, believes and acts well enters the Garden, and is not wronged in the smallest thing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just closed its long sequence of prophets, and this ayah describes what came after them, in general terms rather than about a named community. The commentators note that the passage is about succession rather than about any one people, since the pattern of a generation inheriting a religion and hollowing it out is the one the chapter has been tracing since it turned to the disagreement over Jesus.

keyTerms.note: The verb for losing something through neglect, as one loses property by not looking after it. It does not say they refused the prayer. It says they mislaid it, which is a slower and more familiar failure.
The plural of desire, covering anything wanted strongly. The Quran does not treat these as evil in themselves; the fault named here is following them, making the wanting the thing that decides.
From a root about losing the way and coming to grief through it. The word joins error and its consequence in one term, so what they meet is described as the shape their own wandering took.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabia was inherited like property, and most people practised what their fathers had without examining it. Rites at the sanctuary had drifted far from anything Abraham would have recognised while still being performed with care, and the Quran repeatedly points at that gap. The audience knew what a hollowed inheritance looked like, because they were living inside one and could name the customs that had no reason left behind them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing what happened to the prayer means losing something by neglect, not rejecting it. Arabic uses the same verb for a stray animal and for property allowed to fall into ruin. The Quran chooses it here rather than any of the stronger words available for abandoning or denying, which is what makes the description recognisable rather than remote.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception arrives immediately, which is where the weight of the passage sits. A generation is described in terms that are not dramatic, neglect rather than defiance, and the way back is stated in the next breath and requires three things: turning back, believing, and acting. The closing clause then guards against a fear the exception might create, that a latecomer is admitted on worse terms. Not wronged in the smallest thing means the return is complete.

crossReferences.why: States the same three conditions and adds that bad deeds may be changed into good ones.
Names God as much forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does right and then stays guided.
Tells those who have gone furthest not to despair of the mercy of God at all.

studies.applyIt: Look at the practice you have quietly let slip: not one you decided against, one that simply stopped happening. Name it out loud. Then do the smallest version of it today, badly and late if necessary. The verb in this ayah is about losing something rather than throwing it away, and lost things are usually still where you left them.

studies.title: No Idle Talk But Peace
studies.meaning: The Garden is named and then described by three things, and the first two are absences. It was promised in the unseen, and the promise is called something that will certainly be arrived at. Inside it there is no idle or empty speech, only peace. Provision comes morning and evening. Commentators note how little is described here compared with other passages: no fruit, no rivers, no thrones. What is offered is the removal of noise, a settled rhythm, and the word peace standing where conversation would be.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a community under pressure and to a city full of argument. The commentators note that the surah has just described generations that lost the prayer and followed appetites, and read this passage as the counterpart to that. What is promised is stated as something belonging to the unseen, which is the term for what cannot be verified now and must be taken on the promise itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root about staying put and settling permanently, related to the word for a mine, a place where something remains fixed. The name describes duration rather than beauty, which is why it is chosen here.

Speech that carries nothing: chatter, nonsense, words spent to no purpose. The Quran repeatedly makes its absence a feature of the Garden, which says something about how much of ordinary life it occupies.
The verb for passing property to those who remain. Applied to the Garden it presents entry as receiving what was always going to come to you, rather than as being admitted by a decision at the door.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan life was loud with talk. Poetry contests, market bargaining, tribal boasting and the endless litigation of standing filled the day, and a person's position was made and lost in speech. Food arriving twice a day without being sought was also a specific dream in a place where provision meant caravans, seasons and risk. Both promises in this passage answer things the first audience actually spent their lives managing.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing provision arriving morning and evening occurs twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. Near its opening, Zechariah comes out unable to speak and signals to his people to glorify God morning and evening. Here the same two words mark the rhythm of the Garden. The chapter begins and ends its arc on the same pair of hours.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing the Garden mainly by what is absent is a deliberate strategy. Positive descriptions of an unseen thing quickly become the reader's own imagination, while the removal of idle speech is exact and can be understood without being pictured. The word for inheritance also changes the posture of the reader. What is promised is presented as already assigned, waiting for those it belongs to, rather than as a prize still being competed for.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of hours near this surah's opening, in Zechariah's silent instruction to his people.
Repeats that no idle or sinful speech is heard there, only the saying of peace.
Names the same inheritance, with the heirs being those who turn away from empty talk here.

studies.applyIt: Count roughly how much of what you said today carried nothing: filler, complaint on autopilot, the comment you made to fill a pause. Do not try to stop it. Just take one conversation this week and leave the empty parts out, and see whether the exchange gets shorter or better or both.

studies.title: We Descend Only By Command
studies.meaning: The speaker changes without announcement. Angels are speaking, and the commentators connect the ayah with reports that revelation was once delayed and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) felt the gap, though the sources differ over the details. What they say limits themselves in three directions: they come only by command, everything ahead of them and behind them and between belongs to God, and your Lord is not forgetful. The last clause is the answer. What looked like being overlooked is described as timing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report pauses in revelation during which opponents in the city taunted the Prophet, saying his Lord had left him. Several passages of the Quran are read as answering that taunt. The commentators record more than one account of the specific occasion behind this ayah and treat the general setting as sound while differing over which incident it belongs to.

keyTerms.note: A form suggesting descent in stages rather than at once. Used by the angels of themselves, it matches the manner in which the Quran describes its own arrival, portioned out over years.
Both an order and a matter belonging to someone. The angels place their own movement inside God's command rather than their choice, which is the whole content of what they say here.
An intensive form denied of God. The word is not the ordinary term for forgetting but one describing a disposition, so what is ruled out is the possibility of being the kind who overlooks.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Silence from a patron was the worst news in Arabia. A person under someone's protection who received no word, no answer to a message and no reply to a request, understood that the arrangement had lapsed and that they were now exposed. The taunts in Mecca used exactly that logic. The reply in this ayah does not offer reassurance about feelings; it addresses the reading of a silence.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah's final word denies forgetfulness of God, using an intensive form. The same surah opened with a woman in labour wishing she could become a thing forgotten, using a word from the same root. The chapter that begins with someone longing to be forgotten ends this passage by stating that God does not forget at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah addresses a specific difficulty: how to read a silence from God. Its answer is not that the silence was imagined but that it was governed, and the middle clause makes the reach of that governance total, covering what is ahead, behind and in between. The last word then closes off the interpretation that hurts most. A delay may be many things, and the one thing it is not is a lapse of attention.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same fear directly, saying the Lord has neither forsaken him nor grown to dislike him.
States the same denial in Moses' answer to Pharaoh: my Lord neither errs nor forgets.
Describes the portioned delivery of the recitation, which is the arrangement these angels are stating.

studies.applyIt: Think of a prayer that has gone unanswered long enough that you have stopped mentioning it. Say it once more this week, out loud, without adding an explanation for the delay. The ayah does not say the silence means something good. It says only that it is not because you were forgotten, which is a smaller claim and a more useful one.

studies.title: Be Steadfast In His Service
studies.meaning: The angels' statement closes with a title and an instruction. Lord of the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, so serve Him and be steadfast in serving Him. Commentators note the second verb, which is not the ordinary word for patience but an intensified form meaning to hold out under something that keeps going. Then a question ends the passage without answering it. Do you know for Him any namesake, anyone who bears the name in the way He does.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage in which the angels state that they descend only by command. The commentators connect the sequence with a period when revelation paused and the Prophet was taunted for it, and read this instruction as the practical answer: continue while nothing is arriving. Reports differ over the specific occasion, and the sources give the general setting rather than settling on one incident.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the verb for patience, implying effort maintained against resistance. Arabic marks the difference from ordinary patience by the extra letter, and the Quran uses this form only a few times.

The noun of serving, from the same root as the word for servant. The steadfastness asked for is attached to the practice rather than to circumstances, so what must be endured is the continuing rather than an event.

keyTerms.gloss: a namesake, an equal in name
keyTerms.note: One who bears the same name as another. It occurs twice in the Quran and both are in this surah, once of a boy given a name nobody had carried, once here as a question with no answer offered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names carried weight because they were shared. A man was known by his own name, his father's and his tribe's, and any of them might be held by dozens of others, so a name located you inside a group rather than singling you out. Asking whether anyone bears God's name in the same way used that ordinary fact of Arabian life to make a point that needed no argument.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensified verb used here for holding out steadfastly occurs three times in the Quran, and each time the object is something that continues. Here it is service to God. In another place a household is told to keep to the prayer and endure in it. In the third, a prophet is told to watch his people and hold out while the test he was given runs its course.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is not to worship but to keep worshipping, which is a different request. Devotion that has to be sustained across a silence is treated here as the real thing being asked for, and the intensified verb concedes that it is difficult. The closing question then supplies the reason. If nothing shares the name, nothing else can occupy the place, so persistence is not stubbornness but the only coherent response to what has just been said.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for a namesake, there of a boy given a name nobody carried before.
Gives the same instruction to endure in prayer, with the household told to keep to it.
Answers the closing question of this ayah directly: there is none comparable to Him.

studies.applyIt: Pick the practice you keep restarting and commit to the smallest version of it for two weeks, on the days it feels pointless as much as the days it does not. The word in this ayah is for holding out rather than for beginning, and almost everyone finds the beginning easier than the fourth Tuesday.

studies.title: Does He Not Remember
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted and the reply is a question about memory rather than about power. Does the human being not recall that We created him before, when he was not a thing. Commentators note the verb chosen, which is about remembering rather than knowing, so the answer treats the difficulty as forgetting an event the objector was present for. What follows is an oath and a scene: they will be gathered, and brought around the fire on their knees. The argument and the consequence are given in a single breath.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Denial of bodily resurrection was the standing objection in Mecca, and the Quran answers it repeatedly across the Meccan surahs. The commentators note that the same reply given here was given to Zechariah at the opening of this chapter, when he raised the impossibility of a son and was reminded that he had been created when he was nothing. The surah uses one answer for two very different questions.

keyTerms.note: The verb for recollection rather than for learning. Using it makes the answer an appeal to something already held, so the objector is being asked to retrieve a fact rather than to accept a new one.
An emphatic form of the verb for driving scattered people into one place, used of assembling an army or a herd. It describes collection by force of circumstance rather than by invitation.
Kneeling in the posture of someone waiting on a verdict, not in worship. The word occurs twice in the Quran and both are in this surah, a few ayat apart, describing two different groups.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kneeling was the posture of people awaiting judgement. In an Arabian dispute the parties squatted before whoever was arbitrating, unable to stand and unable to leave, and everyone watching knew what that position meant. The word here does not describe humility. It describes the physical arrangement of a hearing, which is why it needed no explaining to the first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply given to the objector here is the same one given to Zechariah at this surah's opening, in nearly identical words: We created you before, when you were nothing. In the first case it answers a righteous man astonished at good news. In the second it answers a denier of resurrection. The chapter uses one sentence for both, and changes only the tone around it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Treating the objection as forgetfulness rather than as error is the passage's central move. Every person carries evidence of a beginning from nothing, and the argument asks only that they attend to it. That makes the reply available to anyone rather than dependent on scholarship. The scene that follows also fixes the stakes without describing the punishment: they are simply brought around it and made to wait, which is worse than a description would be.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same answer to Zechariah at this surah's opening, about a birth rather than a return.
Traces the objector back to his own origin from a drop, and answers the question about bones.
Asks whether the first creation wearied Us, and notes they remain in doubt about a new one.

studies.applyIt: Try to remember something from before you can remember: your first year, your own birth, the years your parents were alive without you. You cannot, and that is the point. You began, and the beginning is not available to you. Sit with that for a minute rather than arguing with it, and see whether it changes anything.

studies.title: Not One But Will Pass
studies.meaning: The gathering is sorted rather than judged in bulk. From every group the most defiant are drawn out first, and the next line states who is doing the assessing: We know best who most deserves to be scorched there. Then the address turns to everyone. There is not one of you but will come to it, and this is a settled matter with the Lord. Commentators differ over what the passing means, some reading a crossing over, others a coming near or a witnessing, and they record the range without choosing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note that these ayat sit between an argument about resurrection and a description of the rescue that follows, so the sequence runs from denial to sorting to deliverance. No occasion is reported. The address shifts to the second person here for the first time in the passage, which the classical readings take as widening the statement from the objectors to everyone listening.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic verb for extracting something by force from where it is lodged, used of pulling out a tent peg. The sorting is described as removal from a group rather than as a summons.
People who follow the same line, from a root about spreading and being widespread. This exact form occurs once in the Quran, and it names a party defined by what it follows rather than by descent.
From the verb for arriving at water, used of a caravan reaching a well. The word does not settle whether the arrival means entering, and the commentators divide over it for exactly that reason.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arriving at water was the decisive moment of any desert journey. A caravan came to the well, and what happened there, whether they drank or found it dry or fouled, decided everything afterwards. The word this passage uses for coming to the fire is the word for that arrival. For an audience whose survival ran through wells, the image carried the sense of a point everyone must reach and nobody can avoid.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for coming to water in this ayah is used again a few lines later in the same surah, where the guilty are driven to the fire as animals are driven to a watering place. The chapter takes one of the most ordinary events of desert life and uses its vocabulary twice within a few ayat, for two stages of the same day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists on individual assessment inside a collective scene. People are gathered by the parties they belonged to, and then drawn out of them one by one according to a judgement that God keeps to Himself. That cuts against group identity as a shield in both directions, since belonging to the right party will not carry anyone and belonging to the wrong one is not the final word either. What follows in the next ayah is a rescue, which is the shape the passage is building toward.

crossReferences.why: Completes the sentence with the rescue of the God-fearing, in the ayah immediately following.
Uses the same watering vocabulary later in this surah, of the guilty driven to the fire.
Describes the gathering of groups and their acknowledgement, with the Lord's judgement over it.

studies.applyIt: Notice which group you are counting on: a family, a community, people who believe roughly what you believe. There is nothing wrong with belonging. But the passage draws people out of their groups individually, so take one minute to consider what would be left of your account if the group were removed from it.

studies.title: Which Party Has Better Standing
studies.meaning: The rescue is stated in half a line and the wrongdoers are left where they were. Then the scene moves back to this world, and the objection recorded is not an argument at all. Clear signs are recited, and the answer is a comparison of social position: which of the two groups is better placed, and which has the finer gathering. Commentators note that nothing in the reply engages with what was recited. The response to a claim about truth is a remark about who has the better address.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early Muslim community included a high proportion of people without standing, and the classical sources record leading Meccans refusing to sit with them and pointing to the composition of the group as an argument against the message. The commentators read this ayah against that setting, where the comparison being made was visible to anybody in the city.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb for bringing someone safely out of danger, used of survival from drowning or a fall. It describes extraction from a situation already begun rather than protection from entering one.
A place where one stands, extended to social rank. The word covers both a physical location and a station in a community, and the objectors here are using both senses at once.
The place where a community's men met to talk and decide. It occurs only here in the Quran, and Mecca's own assembly hall beside the sanctuary was known by a name from this root.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had an actual assembly hall next to the sanctuary where the heads of clans met, and admission to it marked a man's standing in the city. The objection in this ayah is therefore concrete rather than abstract. It points at who sits in that room and who does not, and the early Muslims, many of them young men, freed slaves and people without powerful families, were mostly not in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for an assembly used here occurs only once in the whole Quran. It names the kind of council that Meccan society ran on, and the city's own meeting hall carried a name from the same root. The objection recorded in this ayah uses the vocabulary of the institution that the objectors themselves controlled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a category error and leaves it standing. A statement about what is true is answered with an observation about who holds position, and the Quran does not refute the observation, which was accurate. The reply comes in the next ayah instead, and it is historical: earlier peoples had better furnishings and appearance and were destroyed anyway. Status is not denied here. It is measured against a longer timescale than the objectors were using.

crossReferences.why: Answers the comparison in the ayah immediately after, by pointing at generations better appointed and gone.
Records the same social objection and the instruction not to drive away those who call on their Lord.
Quotes the reasoning directly: had it been any good, they would not have reached it before us.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself weighing an idea by who holds it: the person's job, their following, how they present. Take one thing you dismissed for that reason and give it half an hour on its own merits this week. The objection in this ayah is one almost everybody makes, and it works because it does not feel like an objection.

studies.title: Better In Goods And Appearance
studies.meaning: The comparison is answered on its own terms. How many generations were destroyed before them who were better in furnishings and better to look at. Commentators note that the two words cover exactly what the objectors had been counting: possessions and the impression they make. The reply that follows is harder. Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend it for him, so that the running of a life without correction is itself described as something granted. What settles the comparison arrives only when the promised thing is seen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Meccan caravans passed the remains of older Arabian settlements on the routes north and south, and the Quran repeatedly directs its audience to look at them. The commentators note that the argument here is not a threat but an appeal to evidence available on any journey, which is why the ayah speaks of generations rather than naming any particular people.

keyTerms.note: Movable property: rugs, vessels, hangings, the things a house is filled with. It occurs twice in the Quran, once of what God has given people in their homes and once here, of people who are gone.

From the verb to see, so how a person or a company strikes the eye. Paired with household goods it covers both what was owned and the impression it made, which is what the objectors had been comparing.
The verb for drawing something out to a greater length, used of stretching rope or extending a term. Applied to a person in error it describes time given rather than help offered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Arabia was visible in exactly these two ways. A rich household showed itself in what filled the tent or the house, the rugs and vessels and cloth that could be seen by any visitor, and in how its people appeared: clothing, mounts, bearing, the size of a company travelling together. The two words in this ayah name the entire vocabulary of Meccan display.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for household furnishings occurs twice in the Quran. In the other place it appears in a list of ordinary blessings, where God is described as giving people goods for their homes to enjoy for a time. The same word therefore names a gift in one passage and the belongings of a vanished generation in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The extension described here is one of the harder ideas in the Quran, and the commentators handle it carefully: continued time in error is not treated as neglect but as something within God's arrangement, and elsewhere the Quran states plainly that a longer rope is not a benefit. The passage also declines to settle the status argument now. It defers the answer to a moment when both parties will see, which leaves the present comparison genuinely undecided.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly: the extension given is not good for them, though it looks it.
Closes this surah with the same question about vanished generations, asking whether any trace is left.
Uses the same word for household goods, there among the ordinary provisions God has given.

studies.applyIt: Walk through your home and pick the object you would be most reluctant to lose that is not needed for anything. Do not get rid of it. Just say out loud what it does for you, honestly, including the part about how it looks to other people. This ayah names possessions and appearance in the same breath, and so do most of us if we listen.

studies.title: The Things That Endure
studies.meaning: Guidance is described as compounding. God increases those who accepted guidance in guidance, so what was received produces more of itself, and the process has no stated end. Then the comparison the objectors had started is answered with a different measure entirely. What lasts, the good deeds, are better with your Lord in reward and better in what they return. Commentators note the phrase, which contrasts what remains with everything the previous ayat had listed as impressive and gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering the comparison of standing and assemblies a few ayat earlier. The commentators connect this phrase about enduring deeds with its only other occurrence in the Quran, in the surah immediately before this one, where it is set directly against wealth and children as the adornment of the present life. Both passages address audiences measuring themselves by what can be counted.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to take up guidance and follow it, so it names a response rather than a state. The ayah gives more of the same thing to those who acted on what they already had.

An active participle from the verb to last, in the feminine plural. It names deeds by their durability rather than their content, which is why the following word has to specify that they are good ones.
The place or manner of returning, from the verb to send back. It measures a deed by what comes back from it, so the comparison being made is about yield rather than about appearance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian wealth was famously perishable. Herds died in drought, caravans were lost, stores were raided, and a family could pass from prosperity to dependence within two seasons. What actually lasted was a reputation for keeping your word and for generosity, remembered in poetry long after the property was gone. The idea of durable good was familiar; this ayah moves the account from a tribe's memory to God's.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing enduring good deeds occurs twice in the Quran, in two consecutive surahs. In the other, it is set directly against wealth and children, which are called the adornment of the present life. Here it answers a comparison of social standing. Both times the same two words are used to shift the measure from what shows to what lasts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as cumulative rather than as a single event, which makes it a direction rather than a status. That fits the surah's earlier warning about a generation that let the prayer slip: what is not built on can also be lost. The second half then supplies a criterion the reader can actually use. Not which deed is largest or most visible, but which one is still there afterwards, and what comes back from it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase in the previous surah, set against wealth and children as passing adornment.
States the same increase: those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and grants their awareness.
Shows the opposite movement earlier in this surah, a generation that let the prayer slip away.

studies.applyIt: List three things you did this month. Then ask of each one what will still be there in ten years: not the thing itself, the effect. Most of what fills a month does not survive that question, and one or two things always do. Do more of the second kind next month, even if they are smaller.

studies.title: I Will Be Given Wealth
studies.meaning: A particular kind of person is put in front of the reader: someone who rejected the signs and then made a confident prediction about his own future prosperity. The reply is two questions rather than a refutation. Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a pledge from the Most Merciful. Commentators note that both would be needed for the claim to stand, and he has neither. What follows is not a denial of his wealth but a record: We will write down what he says, and extend for him what he does not expect.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report the ayat as occurring in connection with a dispute over a debt, in which a wealthy Meccan told a poorer believer that he would have wealth and children in the next life too, and would settle then. Reports vary over the individuals and the details, and the commentators give the general situation as sound while differing on the specifics.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic passive, so he does not say he will earn it but that it will be handed to him. The grammar carries the whole attitude: an expectation of provision without any account of where it comes from.
The verb for climbing to a vantage point and looking over the edge at what is beyond. Applied to the unseen it pictures the only way such a claim could be checked, and asks whether he has done it.
A binding undertaking, of the kind entered publicly between parties. The word returns a few ayat later where intercession is limited to whoever has taken such a pledge with the Most Merciful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan commerce ran on credit and on confidence. A merchant's expectation of a caravan's return underwrote what he could borrow, and a man who spoke confidently about future returns could obtain goods against them. Speaking that way about wealth in the next life applies a familiar commercial posture to a place where no assets exist and no lender operates, which is what makes the two questions in the reply so pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a pledge taken with the Most Merciful appears twice within a few ayat of each other in this surah. Here it is what the confident man does not have. A few lines later it is named as the one thing that gives anybody a claim to intercede. The same word marks what is missing in one case and what is decisive in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a specific kind of presumption: not denial of the next life but the assumption that one's present favour will simply continue there. That is a quieter error than unbelief and considerably more common. The reply also establishes what would be needed to justify such confidence, and the two conditions are exactly the two things no human being possesses. What is left is the record, which the passage says is being written as he speaks.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same attitude at length, in a man who assumes his garden and his standing will continue.
Records the same assumption, that if returned to his Lord he will find the best waiting for him.
Uses the same word for a pledge, there as the condition of any claim to intercede.

studies.applyIt: Notice a place where you assume things will keep going as they are: the income, the health, the arrangement that works. Say out loud, once, that you do not actually know that. Not to frighten yourself. The man in this ayah is not condemned for being wealthy but for speaking about the future as though he had seen it.

studies.title: He Will Come Alone
studies.meaning: What he predicted for himself is taken from him, and the word used is inheritance, so what he spoke of passes to God as property passes at a death. Then the last word of the sentence undoes the rest of it: he comes to Us single. Commentators note the contrast with what he had claimed, since he had named wealth and children and arrives with neither. The next lines widen it. Others took gods to be a source of strength, and those will disown the worship and stand against them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators read these ayat as continuing the case of the confident man in the previous passage and then generalising it to the city's practice at large. Mecca's shrines were understood by many as a source of standing and protection, both for individuals and for clans, and the word used here for what was sought from them names exactly that.

keyTerms.note: The verb for receiving what a person leaves when they are gone. Used here of what he only spoke about, it treats a boast as an estate: something held for a while and then passing out of his hands.
One by itself, with nothing attached. It is the last word of the ayah, and it strips away exactly what he had claimed he would be given, since wealth and children are the two things it excludes.
Power that commands respect and makes a person hard to injure, from a root about being unassailable. It names what the objects of worship were expected to supply rather than any doctrine about them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Mecca was collective and it was purchased. A clan's position rested on its alliances, its numbers and its association with the sanctuary, and being connected to a recognised object of veneration brought prestige and pilgrims. Nobody in that city sought a god for metaphysics; they sought one for exactly what this ayah names, a source of strength that made a family harder to push around.
studies.didYouKnow: The word ending this passage's first ayah, describing a person arriving alone, returns near the end of this surah, where every single being in the heavens and the earth is said to come to the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection alone. What is stated here of one boastful man is stated a few ayat later of everyone without exception.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes an argument about worship out of the realm of belief and puts it in the realm of function. What was sought was strength, and the outcome is described as the exact reverse: the objects turn into opponents. That is the Quran's usual test, applied here at the end rather than in the present. The word for arriving alone then makes the point structurally, since a strategy for standing among people is answered by a scene in which nobody else is present.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same word for arriving alone, there of every creature on the Day of Resurrection.
Names the same motive, gods taken so that they might be helped, and denies that they can help.
States that on the Day they will disown the association, and none informs like the All-Aware.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are relying on to make you hard to knock over: savings, a title, a network, a reputation for being useful. Name one honestly. Then imagine walking into a room where none of it is known and see what you would still have. The last word of this ayah is about arriving with nothing attached.

studies.title: As Guests And As Herds
studies.meaning: An instruction is given in the middle of a warning, and it is aimed at the listener rather than the objectors: do not be in a hurry over them. We are only counting for them a count. Commentators note that the counting is deliberately unspecified, so what looks like delay is described as a tally being kept. Then two arrivals are set side by side. The God-fearing are gathered to the Most Merciful as a delegation is received, and the guilty are driven to the fire the way thirsty animals are driven to water.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a community waiting for a resolution that had not come. The commentators note the instruction against haste as one of a set given during the Meccan period, when believers were under pressure and no relief was in sight. The two images that follow belong to Arabian life directly: the reception of an official delegation, and the driving of a herd to a well.

keyTerms.note: The verb for wanting something before its time. The Quran uses it repeatedly of people impatient for a promised outcome, and here it is addressed to the one waiting rather than to those being waited on.
A party arriving at a ruler's court to be welcomed, mounted and expected. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it makes the arrival an honour extended rather than a summons obeyed.
A herd driven to a well, from the same root used earlier in this surah for coming to the fire. The image is of animals moved by others rather than of people arriving by their own decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both pictures were everyday sights. A delegation arriving at a chief's camp was met, given precedence and provisioned, and everyone knew what it looked like to be received that way. So did everyone know what it looked like to drive a thirsty herd to a well: pressed together, moved from behind, going because they were driven. The two images sort the same event by how a person arrives at it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the God-fearing arriving as a welcomed delegation occurs only once in the whole Quran. So does the word for the guilty being driven to water. The two rare terms sit in consecutive ayat, and each names a way of arriving rather than a destination, so what separates the groups in this passage is the manner of their approach.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction not to hasten reframes waiting itself. A delay in which a count is being kept is not the same as a delay in which nothing is happening, and the passage offers that as the answer to impatience rather than a promise of a date. The two arrivals then make a claim about the Day: it is one event, and the difference between people is not where they end up first but whether they are received or driven.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same watering vocabulary earlier in this surah, of everyone coming to the fire.
Answers the same impatience with an instruction to be patient with a fine patience.
Says the human being was created hasty, and tells them not to ask Him to hurry.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation you want resolved now, where the waiting is the hardest part. Write down what you would do differently if you knew a count was being kept and the number was not yours to see. Then do that one thing this week. The instruction here is not to stop caring; it is to stop rushing.

studies.title: The Heavens Almost Rupture
studies.meaning: Intercession is limited first: nobody holds it except one who has taken a pledge with the Most Merciful. Then a claim is quoted, that the Most Merciful has taken a son, and the response is not an argument but a reaction. You have brought something appalling; the heavens nearly tear at it, the earth splits, the mountains come down. Commentators note that the reply describes creation's response rather than refuting a position, and that the ayah names the attributing itself as what the reaction is to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. More than one claim of divine offspring was current in the environment of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Arabs of the region described the angels as daughters of God, which the Quran answers repeatedly, and Christian communities in Arabia and beyond held a doctrine of divine sonship that they had refined over centuries and understood in their own terms. The commentators note both settings.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make a pair, so joining one's word to another's on their behalf. The Quran does not deny it but places it entirely under permission, which is what the exception in this ayah records.
A very rare word for something enormous and grievous. Its strength is what the commentators dwell on, since the Quran normally answers claims with argument and here it registers a reaction first.
The sound and act of a great structure coming down. Arabic pairs the verb with this noun for emphasis, so the mountains do not merely fall; they fall in the manner of falling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The audience lived among mountains that had not moved in memory. The hills around Mecca were the fixed points of every journey, used for navigation and for marking boundaries, and nothing in the world was more obviously permanent. Describing them as coming down at a sentence used the steadiest thing in the listeners' experience to measure the weight of what had been said.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the claim as appalling occurs only once in the whole Quran. So does the word for the mountains coming down in collapse, in the ayah that follows it. Two of the rarest words in the text sit within two ayat of each other, in a passage that answers with a description of creation's reaction rather than with an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the oneness of God a matter of what creation itself can bear rather than a proposition among others. That is why the reply is a reaction and not a refutation, with the argument coming in the ayat that follow. It should be read alongside the rest of the Quran, which honours Jesus as a prophet, calls Christians the nearest in affection to the believers, and instructs Muslims to dispute with the People of the Book in the best way. The disagreement is stated at full strength; the people are not.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the argument in the ayat immediately after: everyone comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.
Instructs believers to argue with the People of the Book only in the best way, affirming one God.
Answers the parallel Arab claim that God has daughters while they themselves preferred sons.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between disagreeing strongly with a position and thinking less of the people who hold it. The Quran does the first here at full volume, and elsewhere instructs believers to argue in the best way. Pick a disagreement you are in and check which of the two you have been doing, then correct the second while keeping the first.

studies.title: Everyone Comes As A Servant
studies.meaning: The argument arrives after the reaction. It does not befit the Most Merciful to take a son, and the reason follows in the form of a survey. There is not one in the heavens or the earth but comes to the Most Merciful as a servant. He has counted them and numbered them exactly, and each of them arrives on the Day of Resurrection alone. Commentators note that the case is made by inclusion rather than by denial: once every being is placed on one side of the line, no category is left for anybody to occupy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has moved from a claim of divine offspring to this reply, and the commentators read the sequence as deliberate. The chapter has already used the word for servant of Jesus himself, in his own speech from the cradle, so the argument here connects to something the surah established forty ayat earlier rather than being introduced for the first time.

keyTerms.note: The verb for what is appropriate to someone, from a root about seeking. The denial is therefore about what suits the divine nature rather than about what is within divine power, which is a specific kind of claim.

From a root meaning to count with pebbles, the ancient method of exact tallying. It names a count of individuals rather than an estimate of a crowd, which is why the ayah repeats the idea immediately.
One by itself, without company or attachment. It is the last word of the passage and it applies to everyone, so the manner of arrival is the same for all of them however they lived.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian counting was physical. A shepherd tallied a flock with pebbles moved from one hand to another, and a merchant counted stock the same way, one object at a time. The verb this ayah uses comes from that practice. Applied to every being in the heavens and the earth it takes the most concrete and unglamorous form of accounting anyone knew and extends it past any number they could imagine.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for arriving alone appears twice within a few ayat of each other in this surah. First it describes one confident man who had predicted wealth and children for himself and comes with neither. Then it describes every being in the heavens and the earth. What was said about a boaster as a rebuke is repeated about everyone as a plain fact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by universal inclusion, and the term it uses is the one the surah has already applied to Jesus in his own words. That means the point is not made against him but through him: the highest of created beings is described exactly as everyone else is, and the description came first from his own mouth. The exact counting then makes the relation individual rather than collective, so being a servant is not a category anyone is lost inside.

crossReferences.why: Has Jesus open his own speech in this surah with the same word, calling himself God's servant.
States that he would never disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the angels nearest to Him.
Describes coming to God singly, as you were created the first time, leaving everything behind.

studies.applyIt: Try holding two thoughts at once for a minute today: that you are one of an uncountable number, and that you have been counted individually. Most people find one of the two easy and the other hard. The ayah puts them in a single sentence, and the combination is what keeps humility from turning into feeling unimportant.

studies.title: He Will Appoint Love
studies.meaning: A promise about how other people will feel, which is unusual. The Most Merciful will place affection for believers who act well, and the commentators read it in two directions: love from God, and love in the hearts of others towards them. Most allow both. The second ayah then explains the Quran's ease on the tongue by its two purposes, good news for the mindful and warning for a people described as fiercely contentious.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when believers were being boycotted, insulted and in some cases driven out, so a promise of affection was a promise about something they had lost. These are the closing ayat of the surah, which has just described everyone coming to the Merciful alone on the Day. No specific occasion is reported. The word for the hostile people at the end matches the tone of that period.

keyTerms.note: A warm, settled fondness rather than passion or duty, from the same root as one of the divine names. The word is indefinite here, which the commentators read as leaving both its amount and its source open.
A verb of smoothing a path or making something manageable. Applied to the Quran on the tongue, it covers both the ease of reciting it and the ease of holding it in memory.
A rare plural describing people who argue relentlessly and will not be turned. It occurs once in the Quran and names a disposition rather than a belief, so the warning is aimed at obstinacy itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being liked was a form of security in Mecca. Trade depended on people willing to deal with you, marriage on families willing to give, and safety on a clan willing to answer for you. Believers had been losing all three: shopkeepers who would not sell, engagements broken off, relatives publicly disowning them. A promise that affection would be placed in hearts addressed a shortage they could feel daily.
studies.didYouKnow: The name the Most Merciful appears more often in this surah than in any other, which is one reason it has an unusual warmth for a chapter that also contains hard warnings. The promise here is attributed to that name specifically rather than to God under any other, and the ayah names no mechanism for how the love arrives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah promises something the believer cannot produce by effort. Being loved is not an action, so it cannot be earned in the way the preceding clause describes work being done. Placing it in God's hands makes affection a gift rather than a result of charm or usefulness. And it quietly answers a fear specific to religious life, that faithfulness will cost you your place among people. The answer is not that it will not, but that the loss is not final.

crossReferences.why: Says God joined hearts that all the wealth on earth could not have joined.
Repeats the claim that the Quran was made easy for remembrance.
Names affection between people as the only return asked for the message.

studies.applyIt: Name one person who has been unaccountably kind to you, someone with no obligation and nothing to gain. Send them a message today saying so, in plain words, without softening it with a joke. This ayah says affection is placed rather than produced. Acknowledging one instance of it out loud is a way of noticing where it came from.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Or Hear The Faintest Sound
studies.meaning: The surah ends on a question about silence. How many generations were destroyed before them, and can you sense a single one of them, or hear from them so much as a whisper. Commentators note that the question is put to the listener rather than answered, and that the test offered is sensory: not whether their monuments survive, but whether anything of them can be perceived at all. The final word names the smallest sound a person can register, and the chapter closes by asking whether even that is left.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the last ayah of a surah that opened with a whispered prayer. The commentators note that the caravan routes north and south from Mecca passed abandoned settlements, so the question could be tested by anyone in the audience who travelled. The same question about vanished generations appears earlier in this chapter, and the surah returns to it as its closing line.

keyTerms.note: A people joined by living at the same time, from a root about being paired or linked together. It measures history by cohorts of the living rather than by years or by rulers.
The verb behind the word for the senses, so perceiving by sight, sound or touch rather than knowing about. The question asks what is available to the body, not what is recorded in accounts.
A sound so low it is barely registered, a murmur at the edge of hearing. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it sets the threshold of the question as low as the language allows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The silence of an abandoned place was a specific experience for people who travelled. A caravan camping near ruined wells and empty rock dwellings heard nothing but its own animals, in a spot that had once held the noise of a whole town. Travellers on the northern route passed several such places. The question that closes this surah was not rhetorical for them; it described the last night's camp.
studies.didYouKnow: The final word of this surah names the faintest audible sound and occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The chapter's third ayah describes Zechariah calling on his Lord with a call the text calls hidden, using a word from the vocabulary of what cannot be heard. The surah opens with a sound too quiet for people to catch and ends by asking whether any sound is left at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending on a question rather than a statement leaves the reader doing the work, and the test proposed is one anybody can run. Whole peoples with more standing than the present audience have gone past the reach of the senses, which places the comparison of status made earlier in this chapter in its final perspective. The contrast with the surah's opening is also the point: a whisper nobody heard was answered, and the noise of nations is gone.

crossReferences.why: Opens this surah with a call made in secret, the sound at the other end of the chapter's arc.
Asks the same question earlier in this surah, about generations better furnished and better looking.
Describes generations destroyed before them calling out when the time for escape had passed.

studies.applyIt: Say the name of someone four generations back in your own family. Most people cannot. Then notice that you are here because of them, and that the not-knowing has not undone anything they did. Let that settle for a minute before you go back to whatever you were worried about being remembered for.
